name: Alexandre Dessingué
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Alexandre Dessingué studies memory culture and education in Norway, covering how the 2011 terrorist attacks and difficult heritage such as Quisling's grave monument are remembered and memorialised. He also researches critical thinking, dialogic teaching and historical consciousness in primary and secondary schools, using teacher interviews, student surveys and evaluation of teacher development programmes. His work links memory studies, history and social studies didactics, and teacher professional development.

name: Allen Clarence Jones
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Allen Clarence Jones researches creativity and divergent thinking in education, focusing on the design, testing and theory of recombinatory writing games that connect reading with creative writing. The work uses mixed-method action research, pilot testing, iterative game design and framework building, with applications in secondary, primary, multi-grade and ESL classrooms, as well as digital and tabletop formats and sustainability-themed discourse analysis. He also produces creative and literary work, including a longitudinal ethnographic book on a communal group and story and essay collections using Surrealist methods to address social and environmental issues.

name: Anne-Sophie Hufer
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Anne-Sophie Hufer studies multilingual language development in children, focusing on heritage speakers of German in Norway who are also learning Norwegian and English as a foreign language. Her work examines how the heritage language and the majority language influence third-language English, and which linguistic and non-linguistic individual factors shape development across the three languages. The publications describe empirical studies with child learners in an educational setting in Norway.

name: Benedikt Jager
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Benedikt Jager is a literary scholar who works on Scandinavian, especially Norwegian, literature and its links to German-speaking contexts. His publications use close textual analysis and literary-historical and cultural-political approaches to study Romanticism and the Anthropocene (notably Henrik Steffens), literary exchange and censorship in East Germany, contemporary Norwegian comics, war literature and drug-related fiction, and translation under wartime occupation.

name: Brechje Antonet van Osch
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Brechje Antonet van Osch studies heritage and multilingual language use, focusing on grammatical gender, differential object marking, adjective order and cross-linguistic influence in child and adult speakers. Her work combines elicited production tasks, code-switching data, self-paced reading, acceptability judgments and predictive processing measures with heritage languages such as Spanish, Papiamento, Turkish and Portuguese, and with L3/Ln Norwegian. She also writes critical and methodological papers on terminology, monolingual comparison norms and reporting standards in bilingualism research, and contributes to documenting Italo-Romance languages in contact in the Americas.

name: Brita Strand Rangnes
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Brita Strand Rangnes works on literary and public conversation, moderating author talks, panel discussions and debates in Norway. The publications cover contemporary Norwegian fiction, as well as public topics such as menopause, the Anthropocene, luxury consumption, and love and sex in a screen-driven society. One item discusses a book on forms of resistance, including civil disobedience, nonviolence, hunger strikes, activism and the far right.

name: Charlotte Alexandra Wrigley
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Charlotte Alexandra Wrigley studies human and more-than-human relations in landscapes and infrastructures, using humanities and social science approaches such as empirical fieldwork, grey literature analysis, and case studies. Her work covers Arctic permafrost and the subterranean (including the Kola Superdeep Borehole), bird and goose management in aviation safety and conservation, and subsea gas infrastructure such as the Nord Stream leaks. She also writes on fire, soil and heritage, and on species de-extinction and biotechnology, drawing on theories of biopolitics and materiality.

name: Dag Husebø
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Dag Husebø studies teaching and learning in higher education and teacher education in Norway, with a particular focus on action research and sustainability in educational settings. His work uses collaborative action research, curriculum text analysis, and mixed methods that combine course evaluation data, surveys and focus groups. Application areas include STEM teaching quality, mentoring of newly hired university teachers, study programme development, religious education and challenge-based learning.

name: Daniel Aspnes Kristiansen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Daniel Aspnes Kristiansen studies how international students learn Norwegian as a second language in higher education, focusing on motivation, emotions, identity and imagined communities. His publications examine how these factors relate to learning outcomes after a year of study and to students' investment in language learning. He also writes on academic writing and language use in student assignments and on guidance for learners of Norwegian as a second language.

name: Daniel Joe Bowman
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Daniel Joe Bowman studies the cultural history of the automobile through literary analysis, focusing on how horses, dogs and other animals figure in American car culture and the shift from animal to mechanical power. His work draws on novels, poems, periodicals, cartoons and war memoirs, and brings together animal studies, Indigenous studies, environmental humanities and the history of technology. Topics include Indigenous automobility in works by Mathews and Seals, environmental literature of the 1970s, working animals in technological transition, and music and energy culture.

name: David Albert Natvig
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: David Albert Natvig studies phonology, morphology and language contact, with a focus on heritage languages such as American Norwegian and Pennsylvania Dutch. His work combines acoustic and corpus data, census and interview material, and formal models of the syntax–morphology–phonology interface to examine bilingual grammars, allomorphy, language shift and attrition. He also addresses historical sound change in Germanic languages, including umlaut, tonal accent and Verner's Law, and the role of phonological universals.

name: David-Alexandre Thomas Wagner
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: David-Alexandre Thomas Wagner studies history and social studies education in Norway, focusing on dialogic teaching, critical thinking, historical empathy and contextualization, and teachers' epistemic beliefs. His work uses classroom case studies, teacher and student interviews, cognitive interviewing and questionnaire-based surveys, often alongside teacher professional development projects such as CLAE and Partners in Practice. Application areas include primary and secondary schooling, history teacher education, difficult history such as the July 22 attack, film and ChatGPT in the classroom, and education for sustainable development.

name: Dina Lialikhova
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Dolly Jørgensen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Dolly Jørgensen is an environmental historian who studies how museums, exhibitions and archives present extinction, fossil-fuel energy and human-animal relationships. Her work uses historical and critical analysis of museum displays, natural history collections and written records, alongside studies of medieval cultural history, agriculture and soil. Application areas include cultural heritage interpretation, museum practice, extinction and de-extinction debates, and the narration of climate change and industrial history.

name: Eike Christian Heine
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Eike Christian Heine is a historian of technology, science and the environment whose work covers the history of diving and underwater research, the history of archaeological fieldwork, and the relationship between environment, technology and knowledge since the eighteenth century. He also studies how technology museums and heritage institutions present fossil-fuel societies, energy and extraction, drawing on museum studies, public history and exhibition practice. His recent projects address the Carbon Culture exhibition, industrial and urban heritage in Berlin, and heritage responses to flooding and slow environmental change in the Anthropocene.

name: Eric Dean Rasmussen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Eric Dean Rasmussen studies early modern English drama and the history of the printed book, focusing on how texts were annotated, corrected and shaped for readers and theatres in the seventeenth century. His work examines printing-house proof-sheets bound into play quartos and handwritten theatrical annotations in a newly identified copy of the Ben Jonson Second Folio of 1640. He also contributes to scholarly discussion of editing Shakespeare's First Folio and considers the role of annotation in authorship.

name: Eva Stina Maria Jakobsson
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Eva Stina Maria Jakobsson works in environmental and cultural history, with a focus on hydropower, lake and water management, and the historical landscapes of Scandinavia. Her publications include historical studies of conflicts over water levels in Lake Vänern, a lake biography approach, and historical perspectives on sustainable hydropower. She also writes on the history of contraception and menarche, and on tenant farming and a monastery landscape in Norway.

name: Finn Arne Jørgensen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Finn Arne Jørgensen works in environmental history and the environmental humanities, studying how technology shapes relationships between people, animals and places. His publications cover digital surveillance and GPS tracking of wildlife and hunting dogs, digital public histories of spaces, and historical repeat photography and postcards. He also writes on waste and take-back schemes, nuclear power and the Fukushima disaster, and design history, using historical, case-study and comparative approaches.

name: Geir Bergstrøm
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Geir Skeie
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Geir Skeie's publications cover two areas: religious education research and the mechanics of flexible offshore structures. In education, he uses interviews, action research, policy analysis, and narrative and conceptual analysis to study religion and worldviews teaching, pluralism, existential questions, deep learning policy, and bias-based bullying in schools and teacher education. In engineering, he develops semi-analytical cross-section models, supported by finite element checks, for friction, slip and curvature in helically wound pipes, umbilicals and subsea power cables, and contributes to design guidance for upheaval buckling of flexible pipes.

name: Gitte Westergaard
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Gitte Westergaard studies how extinction is displayed and told in museums, focusing on the colonial history behind species loss on islands. Her work uses case studies of preserved animal specimens and cultural objects, such as Saint Lucia giant rice rats, Culebra giant lizards, Hawaiian feather capes and the Pinta Island tortoise, drawing on museology, environmental history and decolonial approaches. She also examines how animal histories are curated across different museum types and comments on de-extinction claims such as the proposed revival of the bluebuck.

name: Hadle Oftedal Andersen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Hadle Oftedal Andersen studies Nordic literature, mainly Norwegian and Nordic poetry from the 1960s onward, along with song lyrics from Norwegian and Danish rock of the 1980s. The work uses close textual analysis informed by phenomenology, deconstruction, ecopoetry, écriture féminine and literary field theory to examine themes such as humour, embodiment, politics and counterculture. Subjects range from French-influenced poetics and the Profil group of writers to new-left radicalism, Finland-Swedish modernist poets and contemporary nature poetry.

name: Inge Særheim
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Inge Særheim studies place names and personal names, mainly from southwestern Norway, using etymological and linguistic interpretation of farm, settlement, island and landscape names. His work also covers names in literature, including novels and local humorous writing, as well as the spelling of place names and its link to identity. Some publications connect names to animals and human history, such as bear hunting and mythical creatures, and others compile name registers for local areas.

name: Ingrid Løland
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Ingrid Løland studies religion in contexts of migration, displacement and diaspora, including Syrian refugees in Norway and Orthodox Christians in the Eritrean diaspora facing transnational repression. Her work draws on qualitative and empirical fieldwork, narrative and metaphor analysis, and perspectives from existential anthropology, political theology and boundary studies. She also writes on biocultural diversity, mountain landscapes and transformative learning in a Kurdish case study, as well as on digital pilgrimage, theorizing in qualitative research, and religion and freedom of expression.

name: Ingrid Nielsen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Ingrid Nielsen studies Scandinavian poetry, with a focus on the sonnet and the sonnet sequence as forms that persist and change over time. Her publications offer close readings of poets such as Olav H. Hauge, Rolf Jacobsen, Ragnvald Skrede, Jon Fosse, Göran Sonnevi and Georg Johannesen, looking at poetic space, rhetoric, lyric song and the relation between the human and the non-human. She also writes on literature and climate activism and contributes introductions, forewords and reviews to edited volumes on poetry.

name: Jacob Lee Tom
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Jacob Lee Tom studies Norwegian literary modernism, examining how it relates to ideas of progress and sustainability. The single publication provided suggests a literary-historical approach centered on Norwegian writers and their thinking about progress, though it does not give details of specific methods or texts.

name: Jan Kristian Hognestad
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Jane Haug Skjoldli
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Jane Haug Skjoldli studies contemporary Norse-oriented religion, especially Heathenry, and how it intersects with popular culture such as video games, television series, music and festivals. Her work combines a survey and follow-up interviews with self-identifying Heathens, qualitative analysis of media and games, and methodological guidance for researching religion and digital games. Topics include religious identity and self-description, links between religion and nature, commercial influence on religious authority, and the use of the Viking and Norse past in heritage and identity.

name: Janne Stigen Drangsholt
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Janne Stigen Drangsholt is a literary scholar and author whose work covers modern and contemporary literature, especially women writers such as Woolf, Undset, Plath, Levy and Mantel. Her publications analyse myth, storytelling, utopia and the representation of the body, ageing and eating disorders in literature, television and popular music, using close reading and cultural criticism. She also writes essays, public talks and exhibition material that bring literary perspectives to a general audience, including crime fiction and the band a-ha.

name: Jon Skarpeid
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Jon Skarpeid works in the study of religion, with a focus on Hinduism and the history of yoga. His publications cover historical introductions to yoga and examine contemporary developments in Hindu thought, including how material things come to be regarded as divine. The work appears to be historical and textual in approach, and is relevant to religious studies and to understanding South Asian religious traditions.

name: Jonas Fossli Gjersø
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Jonas Fossli Gjersø studies the history and political economy of the oil and shipping industries, with a focus on national oil companies, state ownership, political risk and the transfer of petroleum knowledge, including Statoil's international expansion and Sino-Norwegian relations. He also works on imperialism, colonialism and geopolitics, using historical and comparative approaches to topics such as empires, settler colonialism, Greenland, Gaza and Ukraine. Much of this is shared through public talks, panel discussions and commentary aimed at a general audience in Norway.

name: Jonas Taudal Bækgaard
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Ketil Knutsen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Ketil Knutsen works on history education, focusing on historical consciousness and the uses of history, both as a theoretical framework and as a classroom approach. His publications offer a systematic account of how historical awareness shapes society, along with practical guidance for teachers and teacher students on developing pupils' historical consciousness through work with uses of history in school. He has also written on the historical development of subject teacher education (lektorutdanningen) in Norway.

name: Kirsten Johnsen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Kjersti Gjerde Brekklund
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Kjetil Vikhamar Thengs
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Kjetil Vikhamar Thengs studies the historical linguistics of late medieval English, focusing on how language use in local administrative records reflects regional variation and identity. His publications examine churchwardens' accounts and verb forms in local documents, looking at grammatical patterns that anticipate later developments in English. The work draws on close analysis of surviving historical texts from parish and community settings.

name: Marianne Hafnor Bøe
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Marianne Hafnor Bøe studies Islam and Shia Muslim life in Norway and Iran, with attention to gender, religious diversity and political authority. Her work draws on interviews, analysis of public and social media debates, and encyclopedic writing on Iranian politics and religion. Topics include prayer leadership and gender equality among Norwegian Muslims, hospital imam services in public institutions, marriage practices in the Shia diaspora, and the Iranian revolution and protest movements.

name: Marie Lund Stokka
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Marie Lund Stokka studies Norwegian as a heritage language spoken in Latin America, focusing on grammar. Her publications examine the placement of possessives and double definiteness, two noun phrase features of Norwegian, in the speech of heritage speakers. This work falls within linguistics, particularly language contact and heritage language grammar.

name: Marie-Theres Fojuth
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Marie-Theres Fojuth works on museum studies, cultural history and heritage, looking at how museums and exhibitions communicate nature, time, vulnerability and environmental change. Her work covers curating slowness and uncontrollability, exhibitions on mountains, fjords and oceans, and the Anthropocene, alongside historical studies of tourism, postcards and German car travel to Norway. She also develops teaching and outreach on sustainability and ocean heritage, and leads the FJORDS project on museums and fjord ecosystems.

name: Markus Eldegard Mindrebø
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Markus Eldegard Mindrebø studies women, politics and aristocratic social networks in the medieval Old Norse-Icelandic kings' sagas, using network theory and historiographical analysis of kinship, friendship and lordship ties. He also uses strategy video games such as Crusader Kings as simulation tools for qualitative network research, and examines how medieval gender roles and Norse figures are represented in role-playing games and popular culture. His work further includes public talks on how Viking Age women have been remembered and portrayed in medieval sources and in later culture.

name: Matthew Robert Holmes
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Matthew Robert Holmes is a historian of science who studies how animals, plants and microorganisms were managed, introduced and controlled in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, especially within the British Empire and the United States. His archival and case-study work covers colonial agriculture and cotton breeding, biological control of locusts and houseflies with fungi, colonial entomology, invasive species such as sparrows and mongooses, and ideas about animal minds. He also examines the history of genetics, synthetic food and the British debate over genetically modified crops.

name: Melina Antonia Buns
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Melina Antonia Buns is a historian who studies environmental and energy politics in the Nordic region, covering Nordic cooperation, environmental diplomacy and the creation of international environmental law and transboundary pollution agreements. Her work also looks at civil society and social actors, such as anti-nuclear and nature protection movements, and at consumer and trade tensions with European integration. More recent work examines historical energy transitions, uranium mining and its remediation, and the lived and emotional dimensions of energy change.

name: Merja Riitta Stenroos
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Merja Riitta Stenroos studies the history of English, with a focus on Middle English dialect geography, spelling systems and scribal practice. Her work draws on corpus-based analysis of local administrative documents and individual manuscripts, including the Corpus of Middle English Local Documents, to examine regional variation, the localisation of early texts, and how scribes used conventional and variable spellings. She also uses late and post-medieval legal statements as sociolinguistic evidence.

name: Nadine Kolb
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Nadine Kolb studies second and third language acquisition and heritage bilingualism, with a focus on children and on crosslinguistic influence between languages such as Russian, German, English, Spanish and French. Her work uses acceptability judgment tasks, self-paced reading, and classroom surveys, and also includes curriculum comparisons and methodological critiques of bilingualism research. Application areas include English as a foreign language teaching in Germany, plurilingual education policy across Finland, Germany and Norway, immersion education, and language development in refugee children.

name: Narve Dolve
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Narve Dolve works on rhetoric, with a focus on trust, credibility, and reputation in communication and in learning environments. The publications draw on classical Greek and Roman philosophy to look at lying, judgement, conversational behaviour, and the influence of social media influencers. Application areas include education, where teacher reputation and trust affect pupils' learning, and the wider theme of Bildung (danning) in contemporary society.

name: Nina Kalvatn Friestad
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Nina Kalvatn Friestad works on systematic mapping and quality assessment of empirical early childhood education and care (kindergarten) research across Denmark, Norway and Sweden. Her publications track yearly trends in study volume, quality ratings, country and language distribution, research methods, topics and who is studied or used as informants, feeding a database of summaries and topic tags. She has also co-authored a knowledge review on recruiting and retaining teachers in kindergartens and schools.

name: Oliver Martin Traxel
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Oliver Martin Traxel studies Old English and its modern afterlife, looking at how early medieval English texts and vocabulary are adapted, revived and reimagined in contemporary contexts. His work also covers orthography and spelling practices in English, Nordic and constructed languages, as well as the language of fantasy fiction and interactive gamebooks. Methods include textual and philological analysis of medieval manuscripts and linguistic analysis of modern creative and fictional language use.

name: Peter Paul Ferry
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Peter Paul Ferry studies how men and masculinities are represented in literature, ranging from nineteenth-century American sea narratives such as Herman Melville's to contemporary American fiction by George Saunders and post-Troubles Northern Irish writing. His work uses close reading and narrative empathy theory, alongside critical studies of men and masculinities, to examine how texts portray gender, power and trauma. He also applies these ideas to education, considering how close reading in literature classrooms can build students' empathy and help them question restrictive gender norms.

name: Pär Samuel Eliasson
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Pär Samuel Eliasson studies the history of Christianity in India, covering both the major church traditions and present-day Christian practice, ecumenism and theology, including Dalit theology and Christian life under Hindu nationalism. He also works on early modern Jesuit missionary texts in Konkani and Marathi, examining dictionaries, catechism translation and the missionaries' use of Hindu scripture, as well as a Swedish missionary's work among the Bhil people. His work draws on historical and textual analysis within religious studies and missiology.

name: Roald Berg
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Roald Berg studies Norwegian history and foreign policy, with a particular focus on the Svalbard (Spitsbergen) Treaty and the archipelago's geopolitical position. His historical work also covers Norway's foreign relations during the union with Sweden, the concept of neutrality, officers as nation-builders in the 1800s, and the policy and terminology of "Norwegianisation". Further publications address Leiv Eriksson as a colonial icon and the history of the history discipline in Stavanger.

name: Runar Vathne
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Runar Vathne works on professional mentoring in education, covering induction programmes for newly qualified teachers in kindergartens and schools and for newly appointed university staff. His publications describe the NyTi mentoring scheme at the University of Stavanger, school-based teacher education run as partnerships between universities and partner schools and kindergartens, and networks and forums for local mentors. The work is practice-oriented, drawing on school-based action research, experience reports and conference presentations, with an additional contribution on study quality and student influence.

name: Shayan Aqdas
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Shayan Aqdas studies English language teaching and learning in Pakistan, with a focus on reading comprehension and the effects of online instruction on student performance. The work uses schema theory and a person-centered learning framework, applying a comparison of experimental and control groups, comprehension assessments, and questionnaire surveys. Application areas include culturally contextualized classroom materials and preparing higher education institutions for the challenges of remote learning.

name: Sigrid Sandemose
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Sigrid Sandemose works on teacher education and subject-specific didactics, with a focus on practice-oriented learning in the lecturer (lektor) programme at the University of Stavanger. Her publications describe micro-teaching, where student teachers design and test lessons with small pupil groups at university partner schools, and professional guidance within school and kindergarten partnerships. She has also written on literary analysis, examining irony in a literary work called "Eple".

name: Ståle Gundersen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Ståle Gundersen is a philosopher whose work covers philosophy of mind, philosophy of science and philosophy of religion. His publications use conceptual analysis to examine the mind-brain problem, the structure of explanation in Freudian psychoanalysis, and how psychoanalytic theory can be integrated with neuroscience and psychology. He also writes on arguments from consciousness to theism, on qualitative methods, on bias in reasoning, and on intelligent design and mathematics.

name: Suzanne Sophie Ros
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Suzanne Sophie Ros researches energy history and environmental humanities, with a focus on how energy is sensed, lived and embodied in landscapes and infrastructures such as geothermal sites in Iceland and Aotearoa New Zealand. Her methods include historical source analysis of newspapers, reports and surveys, together with fieldwork, sensory walking and interactive installations that involve participants in creating knowledge. She has also studied the growth of environmental concern within Dutch Protestantism from 1960 to 2020 and has written on cultural history as a field.

name: Torill Irene Hestetræet
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Torill Irene Hestetræet researches English language education, with a focus on vocabulary learning and teaching, teachers' beliefs and thinking about vocabulary instruction, and the development of spoken English. Her publications also cover feedback on student writing in English classes and the school topic of democracy and citizenship. The work is oriented toward classroom practice and teacher education in Norwegian schools.

name: Tyson Ashley Retz
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Tyson Ashley Retz works on the philosophy and theory of history, the history of ideas and concepts, and history education. His publications examine the concept of progress and its link to progressive education, the role of questions in producing historical knowledge through R.G. Collingwood's thought, and the use of scale in history teaching, including in the Anthropocene. His work is conceptual and historical, and also covers liberalism and illiberalism, political time, democratic education and historical reenactment.

name: Unni Puntervold Pereira
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Unni Puntervold Pereira studies second language learning, with a focus on how learners' sense of identity and belonging shapes their motivation. Her work, as shown by a 2022 publication, looks at the experiences of learners in a university setting and how feeling included relates to their language learning. The application domain is higher education and the teaching of Norwegian as a second language.

name: Vidar Fagerheim Kalsås
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Vidar Fagerheim Kalsås studies history education in Norway, with a focus on how the Holocaust is taught, including the place of emotions and historical thinking in teachers' lesson planning, based on teacher interviews. He also analyses Norwegian and Nordic history textbooks using postcolonial and Anthropocene-informed analytical questions, examining how colonial entanglements and the climate and nature crisis are presented to pupils. His work further touches on teacher education partnerships and museum and sustainability themes.

name: Yvonne Wilhelmina Henriette van Baal
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Yvonne Wilhelmina Henriette van Baal studies the syntax and morphology of Norwegian noun phrases, focusing on definiteness, double definiteness and grammatical gender. Her work covers heritage Norwegian in North America and dialect variation and change within Norway, using elicited production experiments, corpus data and acceptability judgments alongside formal syntactic analysis. The research also addresses how heritage grammars relate to their baseline varieties, and includes work on multilingualism in education.

name: Anita Berge
summary: Anita Berge studies early childhood education and teacher education, with a focus on children's belonging and participation, inclusion, and teaching for diversity and social justice. Her work includes comparative analysis of national curriculum guidelines across Nordic and European countries, interview-based research on how teacher educators use critical thinking and reflexivity, and studies of how physical spaces and materials shape learning communities in kindergartens. The findings are relevant to kindergarten practice, teacher education programmes and curriculum policy in Norway and internationally.

name: Anne Karin Fotland
summary: Anne Karin Fotland works on kindergarten education in Norway, focusing on staff competence development, collaborative learning and the professional role of kindergarten teachers. Her publications examine study circles as a way of building skills within kindergarten units, based on practitioners' experiences, and look at pedagogical care and developmental support in toddler groups.

name: Anne Kristine Solberg Runestad
summary: Anne Kristine Solberg Runestad works on early childhood teacher education, with a focus on how student teachers develop cultural sensitivity and intercultural competence. Her publications examine sequential event cases as a teaching resource, alongside online learning resources and challenge-based learning approaches. Her work also covers digital tools for early childhood teacher education (ECTE DigiTools), within the context of internationalisation and diversity in higher education.

name: Aud Torill Meland
summary: Aud Torill Meland studies early childhood education in Norway, with a focus on gender, physical activity, care and curriculum content in kindergartens. Her work uses accelerometer measurements, observation, document analysis of annual plans, framework plans and municipal plans, discourse analysis of practicum conversations, and student questionnaires. Application areas include kindergarten staff practice, teacher education and practicum learning, sustainable development in local education policy, and gender balance in higher music education.

name: Barbara Maria Sageidet
summary: Barbara Maria Sageidet studies early childhood education for sustainability, focusing on how preschool children and their teachers learn through gardens, soil activities and urban green spaces in Stavanger, Norway. Her work uses qualitative methods such as observation, interviews, surveys, thematic analysis and mapping, alongside theoretical perspectives from regenerative design, environmental citizenship and philosophy. She also contributes to interdisciplinary research and edited volumes on the Stavanger smart sustainable city, covering policy implementation, cross-disciplinary collaboration and children's understanding of urban issues such as air quality.

name: Beate Gilje Tumyr
summary: Beate Gilje Tumyr studies how music in kindergartens relates to children's health, especially relational health, drawing on music education, music therapy and early childhood pedagogy. Her doctoral work used a phenomenological-hermeneutic approach, with fieldwork, observation and interviews with children and staff analysed through interpretative phenomenological analysis. She also writes about sensory exploration through music and communicates music and health themes to kindergarten practitioners.

name: Bente Gurine Kvitvær Nordmo
summary: Bente Gurine Kvitvær Nordmo studies how the gender of kindergarten staff relates to the physical activity of 3–5-year-old girls and boys in Norwegian outdoor playgrounds. Her work combines accelerometer measurements, systematic observation and semi-structured staff interviews in case studies of a single kindergarten. The findings cover differences in the types of play staff encourage, children's activity levels, and staff attitudes toward gender and the promotion of activity.

name: Bjørn Arild Laland Fuglesten
summary: Bjørn Arild Laland Fuglesten studies how Norwegian kindergartens develop as learning organizations, drawing on Senge's theory and on qualitative interviews analysed with a stepwise-deductive inductive method. His work examines the views of kindergarten owner representatives, preschool directors and pedagogical leaders, covering themes such as leadership, time, vision, staff participation and competence development. He also reports on a project exploring how lower secondary pupils can help recruit men into kindergarten work.

name: Carl Cato Wadel
summary: Carl Cato Wadel studies leadership and organisation in Norwegian kindergartens, including how mergers into larger units change the role of pedagogical leaders and how kindergartens can work as learning organisations. His work is mainly qualitative, based on interviews with pedagogical leaders and kindergarten managers, and draws on profession theory, leadership theory and Senge's learning-organisation perspectives. He also writes on professional learning communities, kindergarten-based competence development, value-based and professional leadership, and recruitment to early childhood teacher education.

name: Dagmar Anita Jakobsen
summary: Dagmar Anita Jakobsen works at the intersection of visual art, art education and early childhood teacher education, focusing on how creative and aesthetic processes can include all children, including those with disabilities. Her work combines artistic development projects, site-specific and performative art productions, and educational case studies, such as a project-based digital microscopy exhibition analysed through thematic analysis of student reflections. Application areas include kindergartens and schools, the Cultural Rucksack programme, teacher training, and Sámi art and culture in education.

name: Elin Kirsti Lie Reikerås
summary: Elin Kirsti Lie Reikerås studies early childhood education and care in Norway and the Nordic countries, covering classroom quality, early cognitive and language development, and children's later academic outcomes. Her work combines longitudinal statistical modelling, such as structural equation modelling, with qualitative case studies, video observation, document analysis, interviews and literature reviews. Further application areas include play with coding toys and computational thinking in early mathematics, special education for children with language difficulties, evaluation policy, and partnerships between universities and kindergartens.

name: Elisabeth Barstad
summary: Elisabeth Barstad works on music, play and aesthetic practices in early childhood education, with a focus on kindergartens. Her publications cover sound environments and noise reduction for children and staff, inclusion through music and movement, and musical confidence among kindergarten teachers. She also writes on partnership-based professional development between the university and kindergartens, using practice-based development work, talks, and articles aimed at practitioners.

name: Eva Marianne Johansson
summary: Eva Marianne Johansson studies children's sense of belonging and exclusion in preschool and early education settings, drawing on Yuval-Davis's theory of the politics of belonging. Her work combines video observation case studies, large surveys of educators and parents across Nordic countries and the Netherlands, and interviews with young children about inclusion and exclusion in play. She also researches how teacher educators in Australia and New Zealand teach for diversity and social justice, using epistemic cognition and reflexivity frameworks, with findings aimed at policy and practice in early childhood and teacher education.

name: Francesca Granone
summary: Francesca Granone studies how young children learn mathematics and computational thinking through play, coding toys, robotics and digital tools in early childhood education and primary school. Her work uses qualitative case studies, video observation, participatory workshops, systematic and scoping literature reviews, and inclusive research methods, often drawing on semiotic and mediated learning theories. It addresses teacher mediation, professional digital competence, and inclusion of children with disabilities and neurodiversity, mainly in Nordic kindergarten settings.

name: Gunnar Magnus Eidsvåg
summary: Gunnar Magnus Eidsvåg studies early childhood education and care (ECEC), with a focus on ethics of care, children's transition from home to kindergarten, and how minority and migrant parents develop belonging through kindergartens. His work uses qualitative interviews, documentary analysis and systematic scoping reviews, alongside philosophical and theological analysis of care ethics in nursing and ECEC. Application areas include Nordic ECEC policy and evaluation, kindergarten quality, digital judgment, religious and worldview diversity, and professional development in kindergartens.

name: Hallgjerd Byrkjeland
summary: Hallgjerd Byrkjeland works on storytelling, children's literature and play, with a focus on how stories move between people, between books and play, and across languages. The publications include essays and reflective accounts of practical work, such as stage-based work with children and embodied storytelling with international students, along with a literary reading of Haugtussa that considers time, experience and memory. Her work appears in both written and performed forms, including cultural contributions at events for early childhood education and university kindergartens.

name: Hans Borge
summary: Hans Borge's listed work, a 2024 publication in Norwegian, addresses decontextualisation as a link between language and mathematics. The title points to research in mathematics education and the role of language in learning mathematical concepts. Only one publication title is available, so the methods and application settings cannot be described in more detail.

name: Helga Vössing-Lahmeyer
summary: Helga Vössing-Lahmeyer works in education research, with a focus on music and sensory exploration in early learning, as seen in a study of how a music box can be explored. She has also carried out a pedagogical analysis for a Norwegian municipality, Eigersund, which points to applied work on local education services. The publications are in Norwegian and relate to kindergarten and school settings.

name: Inger Benny Espedal Tungland
summary: Inger Benny Espedal Tungland studies partnerships between universities and kindergartens or schools, and professional supervision of newly qualified and newly hired teachers, with a focus on kindergarten teacher education. Her work uses qualitative approaches such as action research, hermeneutic analysis and autoethnography, drawing on logs, documents and meeting notes. It addresses practice-based student assignments, quality in mentoring schemes, and development of pedagogical practice in university kindergartens, and includes organising seminars and forums for newly qualified teachers and mentors.

name: Ingunn Berrefjord Ugelstad
summary: Ingunn Berrefjord Ugelstad studies early childhood education and kindergarten practice in Norway, with a focus on outdoor and nature-based activity, physical education, and how sustainability is taught in early childhood teacher education. Her publications also cover health-promoting everyday practices and children's spatial understanding, as well as staff competence development through study circles and support for toddler groups. The work includes views of teachers and parents on increased outdoor time during the Covid-19 outbreak.

name: Joakim Langfjæran
summary: Joakim Langfjæran studies how children aged 4-5 experience freedom, agency, creativity and social interaction when they play freely in video games. The work draws on post-digital thinking, gaming literacy and social semiotics to treat digital play as multimodal meaning-making, using video observation of small groups and video-stimulated recall interviews that treat children as competent participants. The research is aimed at early childhood education, where it may inform how digital play is included in ways that respect children's own initiative.

name: Johana Evelyn Montalvan Castilla
summary: Johana Evelyn Montalvan Castilla studies young children's participation, experiences and learning in smart and sustainable cities, with a focus on Stavanger, Norway. Her work uses qualitative case studies, interviews, observations, conversations with children, surveys and green space mapping to look at urban planning, use of urban green spaces for outdoor learning, and kindergarten STEM education on solar energy. The findings are aimed at teachers, urban planners and policymakers, and she has also worked on pedagogy in higher education.

name: Kari Guttormsen Hempel
summary: Kari Guttormsen Hempel studies migration history with a focus on the role of religion in how migrants settle and integrate. Her work compares Norwegian emigration to the United States after 1870 with Pakistani immigration to Norway after 1970, and includes a biographical case study of a pioneer-era Norwegian woman who moved to Iowa and joined a local Norwegian-American church. Her publications draw on historical and comparative approaches, and she has also taken part in a virtual launch event for a book on a fur trader.

name: Karin Berner
summary: Karin Berner appears to work in early childhood teacher education, as suggested by a 2024 publication titled "Barnehagelærerutdanningen i dag" (Kindergarten teacher education today). Only the title is available, so her methods and specific application areas cannot be described beyond a likely focus on the current state of training for kindergarten teachers in Norway.

name: Kirsten Halle
summary: Kirsten Halle researches music education in kindergartens and schools, with a focus on singing, musicality and collective music-making among children and teachers. Her work uses Cultural-historical Activity Theory to compare studies on teachers' and students' musical self-concept, and it proposes changes to kindergarten teacher education that emphasise collaborative music practice. She also writes about community singing, public health and preparedness, children's aesthetic ways of being, teacher professional identity, and a socially engaged arts project involving a theatre company.

name: Kjersti Lønning Velde
summary: Kjersti Lønning Velde researches early childhood teacher education in Norway, focusing on partnerships between the university and partner kindergartens. Using action research and qualitative, hermeneutic analysis, her work develops practice assignments and supervision approaches that build on kindergarten staff's experiential knowledge and support students' progression in pedagogical leadership. Related publications also address children's participation and well-being and resilience in kindergarten settings.

name: Kristin Fugelsnes
summary: Kristin Fugelsnes studies early childhood education in Norwegian kindergartens, with a focus on children's belonging, inclusion and play across ethnic and cultural differences. Her empirical work draws on video observations of staff–child interactions to examine how staff create conditions for community among children. She also contributes to teacher education, local competence development, trauma-informed care, pedagogical leadership and teaching about violence and abuse against children.

name: Kristin Grøsvik
summary: Kristin Grøsvik studies early childhood education and care in Norway, with a main focus on how kindergarten teachers facilitate children's play and problem-solving with coding toys and other digital tools. Her work uses video observation, workshops, and semi-structured interviews with video-stimulated recall, drawing on sociocultural theory and sustained shared thinking. She also writes on kindergarten teacher education, practice-based research in partnership with a university kindergarten, children's exploration of nature, and everyday kindergarten life.

name: Lars Yngve Rosell
summary: Lars Yngve Rosell studies early childhood education and care (ECEC), focusing on children under three, their participation in the community and their transition from home to kindergarten. His work combines qualitative interviews with teachers, interpreted through a hermeneutic approach, and systematic and scoping reviews of the research literature. It also covers parents' experiences and expectations, pedagogical leadership and the teacher's role during transitions, and how Nordic ECEC coped with and could build resilience after the COVID-19 pandemic.

name: Lisbeth Iversen
summary: Lisbeth Iversen studies early childhood education, focusing on how kindergarten staff act when children are excluded from peer play. Using qualitative methods, mainly observations in kindergartens with children aged 3–6, her work identifies different ways staff approach exclusion situations and how these shape the process and outcome. Related publications examine how staff position themselves in play communities and what they say influences their actions.

name: Maria Dardanou
summary: Maria Dardanou studies how young children learn, play and form ideas about science in museums, science centres and other informal settings. Her work combines the Draw-a-Scientist Test, interviews with children and parents, and mixed quantitative and qualitative analysis to examine children's views of scientists, including gender stereotypes, in an international project. She also looks at children's museums as places for play, exploration and learning about local culture and traditions through art activities, with a focus on early childhood education and care.

name: Maria Fredriksson
summary: Maria Fredriksson studies early childhood education and care (ECEC), focusing on collaboration between kindergartens or preschools and parents, particularly multilingual and minority-background families. Her work uses systematic reviews, review protocols and scoping reviews, alongside project-based research on shared reading and conversation-based literacy practices in kindergarten and home settings. She also writes on children's play and on how national quality initiatives play out in local preschool practice.

name: Marianne Ree
summary: Marianne Ree studies early childhood education and care (ECEC) in Norway and Scandinavia, with a focus on the youngest children's participation, community and wellbeing. Her work uses qualitative interviews with teachers, systematic scoping reviews and research mapping, and it also covers children's transition from home, flexible admission, mealtimes and the first 1000 days of life. The work is aimed at ECEC practice, teacher education and research-practice partnerships.

name: Marianne Undheim
summary: Marianne Undheim studies digital technology in early childhood education and care, especially in Norwegian kindergartens and early childhood teacher education. Her work uses literature reviews, surveys, interviews, focus groups, curriculum and policy document analysis, and video-based case studies of children creating animated stories and digital picture books. Topics include teachers' and teacher educators' professional digital competence, generative AI, digital reading and book choice, children's participation and creativity.

name: Mariella Annika Asikanius
summary: Mariella Annika Asikanius studies early childhood education and care (ECEC) in Norway, with attention to how children under three move from home into ECEC settings. Her work includes a systematic scoping review of research on this transition, as well as publications on play, learning, development and belonging in Norwegian and Brazilian contexts. She also examines migration and transnational belonging, including parents' and staff's perspectives on language dilemmas in ECEC.

name: Marius Rognstad
summary: Marius Rognstad's listed work, a 2025 publication in Norwegian, concerns parent cooperation during the settling-in period in early childhood education and care. It looks at challenges that may arise for both kindergartens and parents as children begin attending. The publication information available does not specify the methods used.

name: Melissa Alejandra Espinoza Ruffo
summary: Melissa Alejandra Espinoza Ruffo studies early childhood education and care, with a focus on how children's sense of belonging and agency are supported. Her work uses a scoping review to map existing research on pedagogical practices and on the role of digital tools and environments in early years settings. The findings apply to educators, program designers and policymakers working in early learning.

name: Monika Kamola
summary: Monika Kamola researches early childhood education and care in Norway, focusing on how teachers support play-based learning with coding toys, including problem solving, computational thinking and mathematics. Her work uses qualitative methods such as video observation, video-stimulated recall interviews, focus groups, action inquiry and cultural probes, drawing on sociocultural and sustained shared thinking perspectives. She also studies children's multisensory and olfactory experiences, and practitioners' views on quality in Nordic kindergartens.

name: Nils Christian Fossdal
summary: Nils Christian Fossdal works in music and performing arts for the very youngest children, leading Elefantteateret's mediation project 100 GLADE dager and taking part in productions with dybwikdans, including an interactive concert for babies. His work is artistic development and practice-based, with performances, workshops, seminars and a book that draw on ideas of wonder, interaction, intra-action and citizenship. He also runs community singing activities called Pubkor for varied groups such as teenagers, men and after-school staff, and his work reaches kindergartens, festivals and local venues in Stavanger.

name: Ove Bergersen
summary: Ove Bergersen studies early childhood education, focusing on garden-based and place-based learning with kindergarten and preschool children, and on how children and teachers talk and explore together. The work uses qualitative methods such as observation, video-recorded conversations, reflexive thematic analysis and walking methodology, within frameworks of sustainability, environmental and rhetorical citizenship, and regenerative design. Application areas include education for sustainable development, soil and ecology learning, early childhood teacher education and intercultural competence.

name: Per Einar Sæbbe
summary: Per Einar Sæbbe studies Norwegian kindergartens and kindergarten teacher education, covering everyday practice, parent cooperation, children's settling-in, friendship and leadership, as well as the history and values of the sector. His work draws on historical document analysis and narrative approaches, alongside studies of workforce recruitment, attrition and men's roles in the profession. The topics are relevant to early childhood education policy, teacher training and kindergarten quality.

name: Sara Esmaeeli
summary: Sara Esmaeeli studies early childhood education and care, including how teacher education prepares future kindergarten teachers to use digital technology with children and how educators view and integrate this topic. Her work also covers children's transition from home to ECEC, the home literacy environment and family risk of reading difficulties in relation to preschool emergent literacy, and the quality, staff experiences and belonging in Norwegian ECEC. She uses systematic and scoping reviews, surveys, focus group interviews and quantitative analysis of child and parent data, with a focus on Norway.

name: Siri Merethe Skar
summary: Siri Merethe Skar researches drama education and its use in teaching and professional development, in Norwegian schools and kindergartens. Her work on lower secondary social studies examines how drama methods such as teacher-in-role and role work can build historical empathy, using a French Revolution drama sequence analysed through dramaturgical production analysis and idea analysis. She also studies improvisation and simulated role situations as a way for kindergarten staff to build professional awareness and inclusive play practices within collective competence development.

name: Stine Elisabeth Vik
summary: Stine Elisabeth Vik studies inclusion, disability and childhood in Norway, using qualitative approaches and document analysis. Her work looks at user-controlled personal assistance for children and youth with disabilities and how independent living principles work within family settings. She also examines special education in preschool teacher education and inclusion and exclusion in interethnic play.

name: Synne Kristin Nese Skarsaune
summary: Synne Kristin Nese Skarsaune studies the inclusion, participation and self-determination of people with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities, including those who communicate through bodily and non-verbal expression. Her work uses ethnography, interviews and phenomenological and philosophical analysis (drawing on Merleau-Ponty, Edith Stein, care ethics and aesthetics) to rethink empathy, user involvement and inclusive research methods. Application areas include professional care services, early childhood education and disability research practice.

name: Tove Erna Belland
summary: Tove Erna Belland studies the transition of children under three from home to early childhood education and care (ECEC), including how parent-active start-up groups can foster children's continuity and belonging. Her work combines a systematic scoping review with qualitative focus group interviews with ECEC teachers, analysed through thematic analysis, and also covers attachment and children's participation. She also examines university-kindergarten partnerships in teacher education, using autoethnographic methods and evaluation of a pilot partnership.

name: Trude Iversen
summary: Trude Iversen researches arts and crafts education in early childhood and teacher education, focusing on children's and students' material encounters with wool, clay, textiles and outdoor places such as forest and shoreline. She uses a-r-t-ography and art-based methods grounded in process philosophy and posthuman thinking, including ideas of worlding and diffraction. Her work connects aesthetic learning, nature-culture relations and sustainability in Nordic kindergarten and teacher training settings.

name: Tuula Helka Sarvas Skarstein
summary: Tuula Helka Sarvas Skarstein studies early childhood education in Norway, with a focus on science learning for toddlers in natural environments, children's critical and higher-order thinking, and mathematics in kindergartens. Her work relies mainly on interviews with early childhood teachers analysed thematically, and also includes mixed methods discussion. She also addresses education for sustainable development, species knowledge and ocean-related hope-based teaching in teacher education, as well as a learning app for movement play.

name: Wilfried Klaas Smidt
summary: Wilfried Klaas Smidt studies early childhood education and care, focusing on preschool teacher wellbeing and burnout, leadership, and the quality of interactions and relationships between teachers and children. His work uses quantitative methods such as latent profile analysis, regression and path analysis, factor analysis of observation tools, and some interviews, with samples mainly from Austrian preschools and also from Germany and wartime Ukraine. He also examines child and teacher personality, structural characteristics of preschools, emergent literacy, transitions to school, and conceptual debates on children's agency and participation.

name: Agnes Wigestrand Hoftun
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Agnes Wigestrand Hoftun studies how Norwegian language students and pre-service teachers handle the Nynorsk written norm, including their own spelling competence and their ability to give spelling guidance on pupil texts. Her methods include a quantitative competence survey with correction tasks and a think-aloud study using screen and audio recordings to examine how online dictionaries are consulted during error correction. The work is relevant to teacher education, dictionary design and language norm policy.

name: Alessandro Falcetta
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Alessandro Falcetta studies the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke's Gospel through philosophical frameworks, including Axel Honneth's theory of recognition and Whitehead's process philosophy, as well as through debates in Norwegian nursing ethics. His work combines biblical scholarship with philosophical and ethical analysis, and applies the parable to questions of care, relationality and ecology. He has also written on the concept of attitudes in Norwegian education law and the national curriculum, and has contributed Norwegian-language public commentary on Israel, Palestine and Gaza and on the idea of 'Norwegian values'.

name: Anastasia Hanukaev
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Anastasia Hanukaev studies intercultural language learning in English as a foreign language classrooms in Norwegian lower secondary schools. Using qualitative case studies built on student texts, focus group interviews and teacher interviews, she examines how an intercultural e-portfolio can support pupils' self-awareness and ability to take others' perspectives. Her work also looks at teachers' views of the e-portfolio and draws out implications for task design and classroom practice.

name: Anders Otterbech Jølbo Myrset
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Anders Otterbech Jølbo Myrset studies second language pragmatics among young learners of English in primary school, focusing on how children understand and produce requests and politeness and how they develop metapragmatic awareness. His work draws on group interviews, task-based discussions, video-prompted discourse completion tests and classroom instruction studies, mainly with Norwegian learners and some comparison with Greek Cypriot learners. It also addresses pragmatics teaching, learner feedback on instruction and the inclusion of pragmatics in primary English teacher education.

name: Andreas Åvitsland
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Andreas Åvitsland studies physical activity, active travel and health among Norwegian adolescents, using data from the School In Motion project. His work applies questionnaires, fitness tests, GIS-based measures of the built environment, decision tree analysis and linear mixed-effect models. Topics include how demographic and environmental factors shape walking, cycling or motorized travel to school, and how cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness relate to health-related quality of life.

name: Ann Elisabeth Laksfoss Cardozo
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Ann Elisabeth Laksfoss Cardozo studies international retirement migration, with a focus on Norwegian and Scandinavian retirees in Alicante, Spain, including the offshoring of publicly funded elderly care, the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, and language use among migrants. Her publications also cover school-university collaboration on environmental citizenship education, as well as historical and critical perspectives on Norway's place in the world, including a work on Francisco Franco. The work draws on a mix of historical and social science approaches to migration, welfare services and education.

name: Arne Jakobsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Arne Jakobsen studies mathematics teacher education and the knowledge teachers need to teach mathematics, with a focus on primary and early-years teaching in Malawi and Norway. His work combines qualitative case studies, thematic analysis, workshops and lesson study interventions with quantitative measurement, including pre/post tests, survey development and cross-national comparison of teacher knowledge instruments. Topics include counting, calculation strategies, mathematical modelling, technology-related teacher knowledge, and multilingual and low-resource classroom settings.

name: Berit Aarrestad
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Berit Aarrestad studies applied drama as an educational approach, focusing on how performance-based learning affects students' critical thinking, cultural identity and political awareness. Her work uses Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore the experiences of Palestinian exchange students taking a drama and intercultural communication course in Norway. It addresses higher education settings, educational reform and the use of drama for self-expression and social activism.

name: Bjørnar Kjellstadli
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Bjørnar Kjellstadli's listed work, titled "Samarbeidslæring gjennom fysisk aktivitet" (Collaborative learning through physical activity), concerns cooperative learning in education and how physical activity can be used as a means of learning. Only a title is available, so the methods and the specific school or age-group settings are not stated. The topic points to application in teaching practice and physical education.

name: Cathrine Holmen Hagum
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Cathrine Holmen Hagum studies student athletes in Norwegian sports high schools, focusing on training load, training distress, injury prevalence and the communication among athletes, coaches, teachers, parents and health personnel. Her work uses quantitative methods, including cross-sectional surveys, questionnaire validation with structural equation modelling, and a randomised controlled trial of individualised, progressive training. The findings are aimed at schools, sports clubs and coaches who manage the combination of elite sport and education, particularly during the transition into high school.

name: Cecilie Aarøe
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Cecilie Aarøe studies the history of German refugees in Denmark at the end of the Second World War, including their time in Danish refugee camps. She works with microhistory, using a singularisation approach that focuses on a single family and draws on oral and written testimonies, and she contributes to methodological debates in that field. Her work also addresses the experiences of children of the enemy who were displaced in 1945.

name: Cecilie Waallann Brown
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Cecilie Waallann Brown studies critical literacy, especially critical visual literacy, as an approach to intercultural learning in English as a foreign language classrooms and teacher education. Her work uses qualitative methods such as case studies, focus group interviews, field notes and thematic analysis, alongside theoretical work, to examine how learners and pre-service teachers read, discuss and redesign images and other multimodal texts. The research is set in Norwegian secondary schools and English teacher education, and also offers pedagogical activities and principles for language teaching.

name: Dag Ove Granås Hovdal
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Dag Ove Granås Hovdal studies physical education in Norwegian secondary schools, focusing on how effort and competitive activities are taught, assessed and experienced by students. His work uses qualitative methods, combining classroom observation, 360-degree and standard video recordings, student written narratives and stimulated recall interviews, analysed thematically within a pragmatist, educational framework. The research addresses teacher assessment practices, learning outcomes and the relevance of PE activities to students' everyday lives.

name: Dag Torvanger
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Eli Flatekval
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Eli Flatekval studies how teacher educators in Norway can build interdisciplinary professional communities for teaching about sustainable development. The research uses an exploratory, participatory qualitative design, analysing audio recordings of interdisciplinary workshops with teacher educators and drawing on transformative learning and dialogue theory. It focuses on how dialogue around concepts such as action competence and systems thinking shapes collaboration in teacher education.

name: Espen Lunde
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Espen Lunde studies how teachers interpret and carry out the practical component of the new oral-practical exam in mathematics and science in Norwegian schools. His work uses interviews with five experienced teachers from different municipalities, covering exam content, time limits, how students can show their competence, and how the exam is organised. The findings point to a need for clearer shared approaches to putting the practical element into operation so that assessment is fair and suitable.

name: Eva Leibinger
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Eva Leibinger studies physical education in primary and secondary schools, focusing on student motivation, perceived competence and enjoyment, and on how teachers put pedagogical models into practice. Her methods include cross-sectional surveys, quantitative analysis of student perceptions, action research with teachers, and a systematic scoping review. She also examines links between physical fitness and health-related quality of life in Norwegian adolescents.

name: Federica Clementi
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Federica Clementi researches diversity, inclusion and democratic participation in two settings: the Norwegian cultural sector and primary-school English language teaching. Her work uses qualitative approaches such as written interviews with cultural practitioners, and arts-based, multimodal and workshop-style teaching practices. It addresses cultural policy, queer-inclusive literacy, intercultural communication and the development of democratic competences in the classroom.

name: Finn Martinsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Finn Martinsen studies teacher education and school development, with a focus on how supervision can link theory and practice for student teachers and support their professional growth. His work uses case studies and school-based action research in long-term partnerships with schools, including collaborative reflection with analytical questions to build teachers' collective capacity to meet pupil diversity. Application areas include inclusive classroom practice, tools for making inclusion concrete, and local competence development for school leaders and teachers.

name: Frode Fanebust
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Frode Fanebust works in Norwegian history and history education, with publications on the Alexander L. Kielland disaster and its aftermath, the myths of the Second World War, free speech during the post-war treason trials, and Greenland's place in great-power politics. He also writes about teacher education, describing a collaboration among the university, a local heritage society and student teachers around the 1825 Restauration emigration, and about cultural history topics such as bread and a newspaper editor's biography. His output includes books, audiobooks, talks and short commentary aimed at both academic and general audiences.

name: Frode Skarstein
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Frode Skarstein works on sustainability and climate change education, covering environmental ethics, teacher education and school-level teaching. His publications include a philosophical analysis of ecocentrism and ethical pluralism, a classroom study of students' talk during climate games, and work on pre-service teachers' views on climate change. He also contributes to interdisciplinary teaching resources, such as Erasmus+ activities combining home economics with STEAM and the Sea Stories of Hope work on ocean education.

name: Gaute Hovtun
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Gaute Hovtun works on mathematics education in Norwegian schools, with a focus on practice-oriented teaching, the "thinking classroom" approach and dialogue-based instruction. His publications also include an analysis of how quadrilaterals are defined in Norwegian primary and lower secondary mathematics textbooks, and material on practising teaching methods and on teachers' experience of not knowing.

name: Hanne Egenæs Staurseth
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hanne Egenæs Staurseth studies teaching and learning in Norwegian schools and teacher education, with a focus on how teachers plan instruction and how pupils talk about and assess texts. Her work uses design-based and action research, drawing on both quantitative and qualitative data, including classroom conversations about texts and moral reasoning. Application areas include the development of an online planning tool for primary and lower secondary teachers, text assessment in lower secondary classrooms, and early teaching practice by first-year student teachers.

name: Hans Erik Bugge
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hans Erik Bugge studies teaching, teacher education and digital technology in Norwegian schools, using design-based research, case studies, interviews, observation and surveys. His work covers online instructional planning tools for teachers, classroom management in technology-rich primary classrooms, critical thinking in dialogic teaching, and the history of teacher education at UiS. He has also applied archetypal psychology to examine how language and imagery help a nation make meaning after collective trauma such as the 22 July attacks.

name: Hans Geir Aasmundsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hans Geir Aasmundsen studies Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity, with a focus on megachurches in Latin America. His work uses comparative case studies of congregations in Buenos Aires, Guatemala City, Asunción and Mexico City, examining leadership, cell group structures, theology, transnational networks, media use, evangelization and growth. A further 2022 publication on narratives and communication suggests an interest in how religious messages are conveyed, though no details of it are available.

name: Hein Berdinesen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hein Berdinesen studies Norwegian schooling, focusing on school leadership, inclusive education, teachers' collective professional development and the organisation of the full-day school. His work combines qualitative studies, using interviews, focus groups, observation and thematic analysis, with literature reviews and philosophical and conceptual analyses of Bildung, climate ethics, educational policy and hermeneutic research methodology.

name: Hildegunn Kalviknes Tessmann
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hildegunn Kalviknes Tessmann studies how creative and artistic methods can help people drive change toward sustainability in higher education. Her work uses utopian future workshops and participatory design to reimagine and physically transform underused areas of a Norwegian university campus, interpreted through American pragmatist thinkers such as Follett, Mead and Dewey. It examines collaboration among multiple stakeholders and the links between research and practice in organizational and cultural transformation, and also touches on physical and virtual exhibition spaces.

name: Håvard Myklebust
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Håvard Myklebust studies the biomechanics of cross-country skiing, using inertial measurement units to capture movement data from well-trained skiers. His work compares uphill V2 skating on asphalt, treadmill and snow, examining hip motion, lateral displacement and pole push timing under controlled speed and incline. The findings relate to how well roller ski training matches on-snow skiing and to possible equipment improvements for Nordic winter sports training.

name: Ingeborg Knævelsrud
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Ingeborg Knævelsrud studies how teacher educators in Norway can build interdisciplinary professional communities for teaching about sustainable development. The work uses an exploratory, participatory qualitative design, analysing audio recordings of interdisciplinary workshops in which the researchers also took part. It draws on transformative learning and dialogue to examine how teacher educators discuss concepts such as action competence, systems thinking and critical thinking.

name: Ingri Dommersnes Jølbo
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Ingri Dommersnes Jølbo researches multilingualism and second-language learning in Norwegian education, covering both school and higher education settings. Her publications examine how newly arrived pupils move from introductory programmes into regular classes, how linguistic diversity can be treated as a resource, and how adult second-language writers, including student teachers, develop academic writing and voice. She also writes about teacher education practice, such as first-year students taking on teaching responsibility in first-grade classrooms.

name: Ingrid Hilmer
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
