Her work combines qualitative, mixed-methods, survey, trial-protocol and systematic or scoping review designs, and also covers research recruitment in chronic illness, older adults' health needs assessment and mHealth for diet in heart failure. She additionally examines nurses' attitudes and self-efficacy in infection prevention with multidrug-resistant bacteria, and co-created digital resources for nursing student mentorship in nursing homes.

name: Anne Marte Løvik
summary: Anne Marte Løvik studies nurse retention and first-line nursing leadership in Norwegian municipal nursing homes. Her work draws on empirical examples and transformational leadership concepts to examine the strategies leaders use to keep nurses in their positions, such as building professional and collegial communities, allowing flexibility and acting as role models. She also contributes to public debate on nursing education policy, including grade requirements for admission to nursing programmes.

name: Anne Schanche Selbekk
summary: Anne Schanche Selbekk studies recovery, peer support and substance use, with attention to mental health and community services. Her work combines qualitative methods (interviews, ethnography, meta-ethnography, discourse and positioning analysis) with quasi-experimental and survey-based quantitative analyses. Application areas include peer-led courses and Recovery Colleges, affected family members and adolescents, violence exposure, open drug scenes, and implementation of cross-sector models for children and young people.

name: Bente Hamre Larsen
summary: Bente Hamre Larsen studies structured, interprofessional health needs assessment of older adults living at home, with a focus on municipal home care services in Norway. Her work combines a systematic review, a scoping review, a pre-post study, a randomized controlled trial protocol and qualitative studies of professionals' experiences to examine effects on quality of life, frailty and healthcare use. She also researches how simulation training and digital or blended education prepare nurses, physiotherapists and occupational therapists to carry out these assessments.

name: Bjørg Karlsen
summary: Bjørg Karlsen's research centres on nurse-assisted eHealth and remote patient monitoring for people with chronic illness, especially heart failure and colorectal cancer after hospital discharge. Her work includes randomised and feasibility trial protocols, mixed methods analyses of nurse work and intervention use, and systematic, integrative and scoping reviews, including a taxonomy of research recruitment in chronic illness studies. She also writes theoretical discussion papers on the concepts of disease and diagnosis in nursing.

name: Britt Marit Haga
summary: Britt Marit Haga conducts qualitative caring science research on health, suffering and meaning in life, with a particular focus on men going through major life changes and transitions. Her work draws on in-depth interviews and focus groups analysed with thematic and phenomenological-hermeneutic methods, grounded in Eriksson's caritative caring theory. She also studies how health professionals reflect on existential concerns among people living with obesity, with relevance for care and support practice.

name: Charlotte Wegener
summary: Charlotte Wegener works on interprofessional health needs assessment for older adults living at home, including the HelseKart project, which covers development, implementation and effects of the approach. Her work includes a randomized controlled trial measuring quality of life, survival, health service use and cost-effectiveness, alongside work on user involvement and social innovation in the public sector. The application setting is municipal health and care services for older people at risk of functional decline.

name: Christophe Eward Kattouw
summary: Christophe Eward Kattouw studies how home care and related services for senior citizens living at home can be reshaped to support independent living. His work uses an idealised design approach with qualitative interviews, content and thematic analysis, and service design workshops involving older people, informal carers, health professionals and managers in Norway. The research compares existing home care with stakeholders' preferred service ecosystem and develops design proposals on timely home care and age-friendly mobility.

name: Eirik Haarr
summary: Eirik Haarr studies opioid prescribing and its consequences in Norway, using national registers, hospital procurement data and tender agreements. His work covers differences between hospital and primary care use of oxycodone and morphine, and risk factors for substance use disorders among people on long-term opioid treatment, analysed with cohort methods and Cox regression. He also writes and speaks on artificial intelligence in medicine, primary care services and tobacco policy for general audiences.

name: Elisabeth Lind Melbye
summary: Elisabeth Lind Melbye studies oral health and care of older adults, including digital tools for nursing home oral care, patient-reported outcomes after dental implant treatment, and interprofessional health needs assessment for home-living older adults. Her methods include cluster randomised and other randomised trials, cross-sectional surveys, questionnaire validation with factor analysis, qualitative interviews, and systematic review with meta-analysis. The work addresses nursing homes, dental implant care, municipal health and care services, and technology acceptance among caregivers.

name: Elisabeth Willumsen
summary: Elisabeth Willumsen researches interprofessional education and collaboration in health and social care, using qualitative and sequential mixed-methods studies with university teachers and senior leaders in Norway and the UK to develop a framework for integrating interprofessional education into curricula. Her work also covers social innovation and community health promotion in elderly care, including nursing homes as community hubs, as well as leadership of innovation in health services, gerontology and memory work with people with cognitive impairment. Much of this is published in Norwegian, including textbooks and chapters on interprofessional collaboration, participation and green social work.

name: Elise Rosenvinge Syse
summary: Elise Rosenvinge Syse studies structured, interprofessional health needs assessment for older adults living at home, centred on the HelseKart project in Norwegian municipalities. Her work combines a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials on quality of life and healthcare use with qualitative fieldwork (shadowing and focus groups) on how the assessment is put into practice. It is framed through social innovation theory and aims to inform guidelines for allocating municipal health and care services.

name: Eva Vabø
summary: Eva Vabø studies supervision and professional formation in nursing education and in a master's programme in professional supervision. Her work combines theoretical and ethical reflection on power and the teacher-student relationship with a qualitative phenomenological-hermeneutic interview study of nursing students' experiences of goal-setting conversations at the start of clinical placements. She also reports on pedagogical development work that uses art-based learning in decentralised education to prompt reflection on ethics and views of humanity.

name: Febe Friberg
summary: Febe Friberg works on nursing knowledge and philosophy, examining relationship-based and person-centred care, nurses' moral notions, and the demands nurses face in everyday practice. Her work uses theoretical and philosophical analysis, phenomenological approaches and an interpretive meta-synthesis of research on implementing person-centred care in Swedish healthcare services. She also addresses research methodology for healthcare studies and doctoral students' development of research competence.

name: Fjoralba Sadja Rama
summary: Fjoralba Sadja Rama studies how people with multiple sclerosis and other chronic illnesses experience working life, including symptom management, mental health, personal resources and openness about their condition at work. Her work examines how work-related conditions relate to employment status and what makes workplaces inclusive, and she has convened an international, interdisciplinary workshop to plan interventions at individual and organisational levels. The publications are mainly conference presentations, talks and research proposals, many in Norwegian, focused on employees' experiences.

name: Flora Nicol Balieva
summary: Flora Nicol Balieva studies the psychological and social burden of skin disease, with a focus on stress, stigmatization, body dysmorphic concerns, depression, anxiety, itch and suicidal ideation. Her work relies mainly on large multicentre cross-sectional studies of dermatology outpatients and controls across Europe, along with a cost survey and a qualitative study in alopecia areata, and it also covers psychodermatology classification and service provision. Conditions examined include hidradenitis suppurativa, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, chronic prurigo, hyperhidrosis and alopecia areata.

name: Gudrun Songøygard Battin
summary: Gudrun Songøygard Battin studies interprofessional teamwork in biopsychosocial rehabilitation for chronic pain, mainly through ethnographic fieldwork combining participant observation and interviews with professionals and patients, analysed thematically. Her work examines how team members negotiate time and workflow, how patients experience encounters with teams in relation to pain stigma, and how shared clinical understandings hold teams together. She also writes on nursing competence in addressing physical health among people with mental health and substance use problems, with a focus on health inequality.

name: Hildegunn Sagvaag
summary: Hildegunn Sagvaag studies recovery, peer support and services for people with substance use and mental health problems, including supported housing, legal frameworks and coercion in municipal care. Her work uses qualitative interviews, narrative and action research approaches, scoping and systematic reviews, and quasi-experimental and multilevel statistical analyses. She also examines alcohol use in workplaces, covering sickness absence and drinking culture, as well as the translation of a peer-led recovery course into a Norwegian setting.

name: Inge Joa
summary: Inge Joa studies psychosis and schizophrenia spectrum disorders, with a focus on early intervention, clinical insight, cognition, childhood trauma and help-seeking. Much of the work draws on the BeSt InTro antipsychotic trial, using regression, mixed-effects and growth curve models to compare amisulpride, aripiprazole and olanzapine and to relate treatment to symptoms, cytokines, cellular adhesion molecules and blood gene expression. She also conducts implementation research, using trials, cohort studies, fidelity measures and qualitative interviews, on evidence-based psychosis treatments, family psychoeducation and a national mental health registry in Norway.

name: Ingrid Elisabeth Mathisen Haaland
summary: Ingrid Elisabeth Mathisen Haaland studies public health nursing in Norway, with a focus on how nurses at child health clinics follow up children and families when there is concern about a child's care. Her work uses qualitative methods, including focus groups and content analysis, to describe nurses' decision-making and the dilemmas they face, and it has led to a proposed model of follow-up for future research. She also contributes to debate on health policy, addressing a municipal commission proposal to remove legal requirements for public health nurses.

name: Ingrid Ølfarnes Røysland
summary: Ingrid Ølfarnes Røysland conducts qualitative health research in two main areas: how adults experience living with unexplained chest pain or microvascular angina while being physically active, and how parental alienation in childhood shapes self-esteem and well-being in adulthood. Her work uses meta-ethnography, phenomenological hermeneutic interviews, secondary analysis with transition theory, and narrative case approaches. The findings are aimed at person-centred care, nursing practice, and support from health, social care and educational services.

name: Jorunn Nærland Skjærpe
summary: Jorunn Nærland Skjærpe studies care for people with serious mental illness and for older adults living at home, mainly in Norwegian municipal and community health services. Her work uses qualitative interviews, café dialogues and co-creation workshops, along with a feasibility study, a randomized trial protocol, and systematic and realist review protocols. Topics include care coordination, determinants of health, digital peer support apps such as DigiPer, health needs assessment, and parent-focused oral health interventions for young children.

name: Kristin Hjorthaug
summary: Kristin Hjorthaug studies nursing education and professional development, with a focus on digital storytelling as a way to support reflection in clinical practice. Her work uses exploratory qualitative methods, including focus group interviews analysed through content analysis, to examine how practicing nurses in hospital and nursing home settings respond to digital stories made by nursing students. The research relates to continuing education for nurses and ways of embedding reflective learning activities in everyday clinical units.

name: Kristin Hjorthaug Urstad
summary: Kristin Hjorthaug Urstad's publications cover health literacy and patient self-management, eHealth support after hospital discharge, and simulation-based nursing and midwifery education. Her work includes randomized trials, quasi-experimental, cross-sectional and qualitative studies, scoping and integrative reviews, and a meta-synthesis. Settings include kidney transplantation, colorectal cancer, heart failure, primary care, parents of toddlers, adolescent health messaging, and nursing education in Norway, Tanzania and Malawi.

name: Linda Horne Mæland
summary: Linda Horne Mæland studies why nurses stay in practice, focusing on Norwegian school nurses, nursing home nurses and mental health nurses. Her work uses qualitative designs, mainly in-depth and focus group interviews analysed with hermeneutic and phenomenological methods. Topics include self-realization, self-care, good work-life, first-line leaders' retention strategies informed by transformational leadership, and nurses' aspirations for public health nursing education.

name: Lise Sæstad Beyene
summary: Lise Sæstad Beyene studies mental healthcare and mental health nursing, with a focus on medication-free treatment, milieu therapy, and relational competence between professionals and patients. Her work uses qualitative designs such as focus groups, interviews and thematic analysis, alongside scoping and integrative reviews, in Norwegian inpatient wards, community mental health services and primary care courses. Other topics include nurses' self-care, shared decision-making and patient participation, physical health in people with mental health and substance use problems, and nursing education.

name: Magnus Jørgensen
summary: Magnus Jørgensen studies how socioeconomic background, life transitions and health behaviors relate to depressed mood, life satisfaction and self-esteem from adolescence into midlife, mainly using long-running Norwegian cohort data. His work applies longitudinal statistical models such as latent growth, cross-lagged panel and Bayesian structural equation models, and also covers adolescent academic performance, including gaming, self-beliefs and social support. He has additionally run a survey-based conjoint analysis of public preferences for how psychologists present themselves online.

name: Marianne Storm
summary: Marianne Storm studies digital and community-based health care, with a focus on people with serious mental illness, older adults living at home, and patients with long-term conditions such as heart failure. Her work combines qualitative interviews, co-creation and simulation methods, systematic and scoping reviews, longitudinal surveys, and randomized and feasibility trials. Application areas include digital peer support, remote patient monitoring, health needs assessment, housing and service organisation, nursing workforce experiences and infection prevention.

name: Marie Undheim
summary: Marie Undheim studies nursing education, focusing on blended learning and clinical skills training for bachelor's nursing students at satellite campuses in rural Southern Norway. Her work includes a cross-sectional survey study of student satisfaction and self-confidence, analysed with descriptive statistics and content analysis. She also shares experience with simulation and video-recording tools in skills training and with flexible, district-friendly nursing programmes in the Ryfylke region.

name: Marit Alstveit
summary: Marit Alstveit studies public health nursing, with a focus on postnatal care for new families and on public health nurse education. Her work uses qualitative methods, including phenomenological interviews with mothers and fathers, a meta-ethnography of nurses' perspectives, and a comparison of national legislation across the Nordic countries. It applies to child and family health centres, municipal postnatal services, and nursing education.

name: Marte Johanne Tangeraas Hansen
summary: Marte Johanne Tangeraas Hansen studies hospital nurses' attitudes, knowledge and self-efficacy when caring for patients with multidrug-resistant bacteria, with attention to infection prevention and control and antibiotic stewardship. Her work in a Norwegian university hospital combines repeated questionnaire surveys, serial focus group interviews and convergent mixed-methods analysis, following nurses before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings address organisational barriers, nurses' role in stewardship and workforce resilience, with relevance to clinical practice, nursing education and health policy.

name: Morten Munkvik
summary: Morten Munkvik writes on the use of artificial intelligence in general practice and primary care, including how AI-generated clinical notes should be labelled and how such tools can be applied in a structured way. His publications also address health policy for the Norwegian GP system, notably patient-adjusted basic funding and its possible effects on the GP scheme. Further work covers clinical case discussion and a group- and activity-based learning model for medical education.

name: Ole Tjomsland
summary: Ole Tjomsland studies health services quality and governance in Norwegian specialist healthcare, with a focus on unwarranted variation, overuse of low-value procedures and patient safety. His work combines national registry analyses, intervention protocols, clinical dashboard development, policy frameworks and qualitative interviews with surgeons about adverse events and external oversight. Application areas include cardiology, orthopaedics, endoscopy, robotic surgery and hospital leadership, along with some writing on medical ethics and waiting lists.

name: Per Christer Thomas Westergren
summary: Per Christer Thomas Westergren studies child and adolescent health and the nursing and primary care that supports it, mainly in Norway. The work combines qualitative studies (observations, interviews, focus groups) and evidence syntheses such as meta-ethnographies, scoping and umbrella reviews with cross-sectional quantitative analyses of quality of life, mental health, socioeconomic status and obesity. Application areas include online screening in well-child and school health services, parents' health information use, transitions of care, and nursing history.

name: Randi Wågø Aas
summary: Randi Wågø Aas studies work participation and public health, focusing on return to work after long-term sick leave, alcohol use and workplace culture, and school participation among young people. Her work uses large-scale qualitative interviews analysed with content analysis and frameworks such as the WHO ICF and the Model of Human Occupation, alongside cross-sectional surveys, multilevel and regression analyses, and a systematic review with meta-analysis. Application areas include sickness absence follow-up, occupational health services, workplace alcohol prevention, and school dropout and health promotion in Norwegian schools.

name: Rita Helene Bügelmeyer
summary: Rita Helene Bügelmeyer works on nursing education and nursing practice, based on two 2022 publications in Norwegian. One looks at how international placements for nursing students can be planned and carried out. The other covers how wound care nurses shared experiences through a resource network, pointing to professional knowledge exchange in clinical nursing.

name: Rosalynn Austin
summary: Rosalynn Austin researches heart failure care, with a focus on heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) services in the UK and on nurse-supported digital health for people with chronic illness. Her work uses scoping and systematic reviews, consensus surveys, mixed methods analyses and a randomised trial protocol to study service provision, remote patient monitoring, diet-focused mHealth apps and research recruitment. Other publications cover medication review in advanced kidney disease and sex and gender in cardiovascular research.

name: Stig Erlend Bjønness
summary: Stig Erlend Bjønness studies mental health services for young people and other vulnerable groups in Norway, with a focus on refugee, national minority, Indigenous and adolescent populations. His work uses qualitative interviews, systematic reviews and a mixed methods project protocol that includes a cohort and a randomized trial. It addresses access to care, user involvement and shared decision-making, culturally sensitive and digital services, and low-threshold support for people who use drugs.

name: Terese Elisabet Bondas
summary: Terese Elisabet Bondas studies maternal, child and family health, with a focus on public health nursing, postnatal care, fatherhood, and the prevention of child neglect. Her work mainly uses qualitative methods such as focus groups, interviews, reflexive thematic analysis and phenomenological approaches, together with many meta-ethnographic syntheses of existing studies. These syntheses cover topics including alcohol use in pregnancy, LGBTQ+ parenthood, refugee youth sexual health and family life with youth substance use, and she also writes on methodology for meta-ethnography and on multicultural doula care for immigrant women.

name: Torgeir Gilje Lid
summary: Torgeir Gilje Lid studies alcohol use, substance use disorders and chronic pain in primary care and addiction treatment settings, mainly in Norway. The publications combine randomised and pilot trials, feasibility and implementation studies with qualitative interviews, population survey analyses from the Tromsø Study, and national prescribing and registry data. Applications include alcohol case finding by general practitioners, smoking, exercise and nutrition support for people in opioid agonist therapy, amphetamine dependence treatment, opioid prescribing trends, and multidisciplinary pain management.

name: Trond Erik Grønnestad
summary: Trond Erik Grønnestad conducts mainly qualitative research (interviews, focus groups and ethnographic fieldwork) on health and social services for people who use drugs or live with co-occurring severe mental illness and substance use disorders. His work covers public gathering places and open drug scenes in Norway and Denmark, as well as legal rights, coercion and decision support in municipal housing and care services. He has also studied shared decision-making in adolescent inpatient mental healthcare and young people's experiences of bereavement groups.

name: Unn Elisabeth Hammervold
summary: Unn Elisabeth Hammervold studies mental health and substance use care, focusing on supported housing and service organisation for people with co-occurring substance use and mental health problems, including recovery and health promotion in the Nordic context. Her work also covers how relational competence is taught in mental health education for healthcare professionals, and patients' experiences of post-incident reviews after restraint in acute psychiatric care. She uses scoping reviews with systematic database searches and thematic analysis, alongside qualitative interviews with patients.

name: Adriana Rosenberg
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Adriana Rosenberg studies patient safety and education in healthcare, with a focus on how national, system-wide safety investigations are carried out and how investigators are trained. Her work uses qualitative methods, including individual and focus group interviews analysed thematically, to evaluate a master's level course in Norway. The findings inform the design of curricula for independent safety investigators in health services.

name: Aina Lillian Bjerkeli Lekens
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Aina Lillian Bjerkeli Lekens studies nurse anaesthesia practice, focusing on how nursing care, person-centred and holistic care, and professional competence are enacted around surgical and anaesthetised patients. Her work uses qualitative methods such as focused ethnography, interviews, content and reflexive thematic analysis, and meta-ethnographic synthesis, alongside philosophical analysis of the concepts of person and care. She also writes on nurse anaesthetists' pandemic redeployment, evidence-based clinical guidance for lung recruitment during general anaesthesia, supervision of students and the development of the profession in Norway.

name: Anders Batman Mjelle
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Anders Batman Mjelle conducts clinical research in paediatrics, neonatology and infection, including bacterial meningitis in children, C-reactive protein and monitoring strategies for term newborns after prolonged rupture of membranes, and antibiotic use for childhood respiratory infections in primary care. The work also covers ultrasound, with a Nordic survey of its use and training in anesthesiology and a follow-up study of liver stiffness measured by elastography after hepatitis C treatment. Methods include retrospective record reviews, prospective observational studies and cross-sectional surveys in Norwegian and Nordic healthcare settings.

name: Anders Blilie
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Anders Blilie works on artificial intelligence for digital pathology of prostate cancer, building and validating deep learning models that detect cancer, assign Gleason grades and identify cribriform morphology in whole slide images of biopsies. His work tests how well these models hold up across laboratories, scanners and populations, using approaches such as physical color calibration, tissue detection comparison, conformal prediction for flagging unreliable outputs, and external validation on a Middle Eastern cohort with a released public dataset. He also studies clinical uses such as reducing immunohistochemistry staining, and has written a pre-specified validation protocol and compared prostatectomy tissue biobanking protocols.

name: Anita Salamonsen
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Anita Salamonsen studies mental health services and wellbeing for young people, particularly adolescents with refugee or asylum-seeker backgrounds and national minority and Indigenous (Sámi) youth in Norway. Her work uses qualitative interviews, systematic reviews, mixed methods and participatory action research to examine help-seeking, mental health literacy, cultural adaptation of services, digital services and user involvement in treatment. She also writes on arts, culture and creative wellbeing, including Sámi yoik, accessible theatre performances, and the influence of interview location on qualitative research.

name: Anne Lene Høivik
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Anne Lene Høivik researches patient safety and resilience in healthcare, focusing on how emergency departments cope with the major organisational change of relocating a hospital. Her doctoral project uses a longitudinal case study design with semi-structured interviews, document analysis and participant observation, including observation of simulations and tests, to follow work practice before, during and after the move. She has also been associated with a simulation-based intensive course, SimCamp2023.

name: Asma Sabri
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Asma Sabri studies person-centred practice and patient experience across the stroke care pathway, with a focus on transitions between healthcare settings and the period after hospital discharge. Her methods include qualitative interviews, patient journey mapping, scoping reviews, mixed methods designs and concept analysis, with work on stroke teams, multiteam systems and resilience in complex patient pathways. She has also carried out a quantitative survey of patient safety culture among primary care professionals in Morocco.

name: Ayyad Ahmad Zartasht Khan
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Ayyad Ahmad Zartasht Khan studies dry eye disease and meibomian gland dysfunction, mainly through analysis of a large Norwegian specialist clinic cohort, and also through systematic and narrative reviews. The work covers symptom and tear film patterns by age, sex and time of day, risk factors, treatment response to topical dexamethasone and intense pulsed light, and drug-related effects such as isotretinoin. Other publications cover tear-fluid glycoproteomics of galectin-3 and lacritin binding, scar minimization in oculoplastic surgery (brow lift, blepharoplasty, epicanthoplasty, dacryocystorhinostomy), and clinical case reports on Demodex and meningococcal infection.

name: Birte Fagerdal
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Birte Fagerdal studies resilience in healthcare, focusing on how hospital teams adapt to demand and capacity pressures and how team, organizational and health system factors shape that adaptation. Her work uses qualitative methods such as observation, interviews, focus groups, case studies, stakeholder analysis and participatory workshops in hospitals, nursing homes and home care. She also develops and tests learning tools and frameworks for turning resilience theory into practice, and examines the role of champions and leaders in quality improvement.

name: Bjørg Frøysland Oftedal
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Bjørg Frøysland Oftedal studies nursing and health professional practice, using mainly qualitative methods such as interviews, hermeneutic and discourse analysis, alongside randomized and observational intervention studies. Her work covers school nurses' work-life and reasons for staying in practice, primary care follow-up and self-management support for people at risk of type 2 diabetes, and interprofessional collaboration. She also examines simulation-based training for newborn resuscitation in a rural Tanzanian hospital, the competence of health professionals with master's degrees, and the use of simulation in nursing education.

name: Bodil Bø
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Bodil Bø studies nursing and midwifery education and practice, with a strong focus on simulation-based education in low-resource settings in Malawi, Tanzania, Madagascar and wider sub-Saharan Africa. Her work combines qualitative interviews and focus groups, randomised and quasi-experimental trials, mixed-methods studies, meta-synthesis and psychometric scale validation. She also examines spiritual and existential care through competency assessment tools for students and analysis of Norwegian health policy documents, and has studied postoperative nursing care in a conflict-affected hospital in Nigeria.

name: Britt Sætre Hansen
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Britt Sætre Hansen studies nursing practice and education in anaesthesia, critical care, perioperative and cancer care settings, mainly in Norway. Her work uses qualitative designs (interviews, focus groups, focused ethnography, Delphi surveys) and evidence syntheses such as meta-ethnography, scoping and integrative reviews, alongside hospital-based pre-post and mortality review studies. Topics include nurse anaesthetists' holistic care, competence assessment of postgraduate students in placement, non-technical skills of operating room nurses, simulation training for stroke thrombectomy teams, rapid response systems, and breast cancer survivors' return to work.

name: Camilla Jacqueline Hansine Normand
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Camilla Jacqueline Hansine Normand studies the use of cardiac resynchronization therapy and other implantable cardiac devices in heart failure, drawing on European registries and the ESC CRT Surveys. Her work examines clinical, organisational, economic and socioeconomic factors behind who receives devices, upgrade versus new implantation outcomes, and external validation of a machine learning mortality risk score. She also contributes to medical education research, including a scoping review of educational supervision in internal medicine residency and work on simulation of orthopaedic surgical technique.

name: Caroline Guldberg Fugelli
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Caroline Guldberg Fugelli researches simulation-based training for multidisciplinary teams delivering endovascular thrombectomy for acute ischaemic stroke, with a focus on anaesthesia in non-operating room settings. She combines pre-post interventional cohort studies of workflow times, anaesthetic management and patient functional outcomes with focus group interviews analysed by qualitative content analysis. Her work examines how training design and the make-up of the teaching faculty, especially including anaesthesia professionals, relate to care processes and outcomes in stroke treatment.

name: Cecilie Haraldseid-Driftland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Cecilie Haraldseid-Driftland studies resilience in healthcare as a multilevel phenomenon, covering how individuals, teams, leaders, organisations and policymakers adapt to workforce shortages and rising care demands, particularly in elderly, home and nursing care. Her work combines qualitative focus group studies, systematic reviews, survey instrument development with psychometric validation, and participatory co-design of learning tools and leadership toolboxes. It also addresses staff mental well-being, leadership support, collaborative learning and stakeholder involvement, and the translation of resilience theory into practical frameworks for healthcare quality and safety.

name: Charity Atim Fabio Ambrose
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Charity Atim Fabio Ambrose studies how refugees from African countries, both young people and their parents, experience municipal mental health services in Norway. Her work uses qualitative interviews analysed thematically to examine trust, cultural differences, stigma, language barriers and fear of child welfare involvement as obstacles to care. The findings point to applications in culturally responsive health care, professional interpreter use and more equitable services for refugee families.

name: Charles Julian Thompson
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Charles Julian Thompson studies major trauma care and outcomes, using randomised trials, national audit data and machine-learning causal models. His work covers prehospital interventions such as intubation and blood product transfusion, emergency department procedures including REBOA and chest drains, and the effect of frailty and geriatric assessment on survival in older trauma patients. He also examines clinical decision-making and cognitive bias, population-level trauma trends during COVID-19, intensive care risk prediction in brain injury, and psychological and domestic violence aspects of injury.

name: Clemens Weber
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Clemens Weber studies surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis, mainly through randomized trials and secondary analyses of the NORDSTEN trials, comparing decompression techniques, decompression with or without fusion, and predictors of patient-reported outcomes. He also uses Norwegian trauma registry and hospital data to describe the epidemiology and mortality of traumatic brain injury and the design of registry inclusion criteria. Further work compares navigated and conventional pedicle screw placement in thoracolumbar and cervical spine injuries.

name: Dagrunn Nåden Dyrstad
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Dagrunn Nåden Dyrstad studies nursing and health professions education, with a focus on how students' clinical competence is assessed in placement and how simulation, including virtual simulation, supports learning. Her work uses qualitative interviews, focus groups, document analysis and literature reviews, covering postgraduate critical care nursing students, preceptors and teachers, and supervisors such as midwives and specialist nurses. She also examines interprofessional simulation training for health needs assessment of older adults living at home, including course development and training approaches for community healthcare professionals.

name: Daniel Adrian Lungu
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Daniel Adrian Lungu studies the mental wellbeing and resilience of older adult care workers, leaders and informal caregivers, using qualitative interviews, systematic reviews, and mixed-methods co-design protocols across several countries. He also works on public health risk communication, including randomized experiments and interview studies on how people understand pandemic videos and information, and on health measurement and digital health, such as questionnaire development for smell disorders, a lifestyle app evaluation, and digital stress and burnout in academia. Further work covers contraceptive prescribing practices for adolescents and purpose-driven social innovation in care for frail people.

name: David Westfall Bates
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: David Westfall Bates studies how artificial intelligence and electronic health record data can be used and governed in clinical care. His publications include multisite cohort studies, surveys and systematic reviews on AI scribes, generative language models, monitoring of AI performance over time, and methods for extracting information from clinical notes. He also examines patient safety, diagnostic error, language-related disparities in surgical readmission, opioid prescribing trends and the effects of AI on medical training.

name: Eldar Søreide
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Eldar Søreide's publications cover two main areas: outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and the quality, safety and organisation of hospital care. The cardiac arrest work uses pooled randomised trial data, registry analyses and long-term follow-up with questionnaires to study prognostic factors such as electrolyte disorders, circulatory shock and pupillometry, together with survivor quality of life. The health services work includes international observational studies of end-of-life decisions and communication in intensive care units, qualitative interviews with surgeons about adverse events, mortality review of a rapid response system, and clinical dashboards and audits aimed at reducing unwarranted variation in Norwegian hospitals.

name: Elin Espeland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Elin Espeland studies nursing education, with a focus on how digital tools support students learning clinical skills. Her work includes a qualitative focus group study of second-year nursing students using an interactive skills training app, and a related piece describing a multilingual app covering nursing procedures. She also has a publication on wound care nurses sharing experiences in a resource network, indicating interest in professional practice and knowledge sharing in nursing.

name: Eline Ree
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Eline Ree studies resilience in healthcare, with a focus on long-term and older adult care, and on how managers, leaders and staff champions support adaptive, high-quality services. Her work combines qualitative interviews, case studies, systematic reviews, stakeholder analysis, survey instrument development and validation, and cross-country policy comparison. She also researches mental health and service experiences of refugee, minority and Indigenous youth and parents in Norway, including a digital mental health project and a leader toolbox for care workforce well-being.

name: Ellinor Christin Haukland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Ellinor Christin Haukland studies the care of patients with advanced cancer, including palliative and stereotactic radiotherapy for brain and bone metastases, immune checkpoint inhibitors and chemotherapy for several tumour types. Her work relies mainly on retrospective, real-world and register-based cohort analyses of survival, prognostic factors, toxicity and patterns of care in Norway, along with a cluster-randomised trial of early palliative care in oncology. Further topics include patient-reported symptoms, caregiver satisfaction, quality indicators and health technology for the hospital-to-home transition.

name: Frederikke Buskov
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Frederikke Buskov studies newborn care around the time of birth, covering resuscitation in the delivery room and the care of preterm infants in neonatal intensive care. Her work uses randomized trials, prospective observational studies, video analysis, dry-electrode ECG heart rate data and systematic review methods to examine heart rate monitoring, ventilation, tactile stimulation, pulse oximetry and umbilical pH. It also covers early skin-to-skin contact for preterm infants and the methodological problem of selection bias in a resuscitation trial that relied on video recordings.

name: Gerhard Peter Dieckmann
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Gerhard Peter Dieckmann's publications focus on simulation-based education in health professions, including debriefing methods that address complexity and resilience, facilitator preparation and competence, and the work of simulated and standardized patients. He also studies escape rooms, extended reality and clinical leadership training, and examines AI in healthcare through student over-reliance and bias in AI-generated depictions of leadership. His methods include mixed-methods and qualitative studies, design-based research, scoping reviews, consensus meetings, instrument validation and cross-sectional analyses.

name: Hanne Markhus Lillevik
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Hanne Markhus Lillevik studies newborn care, with work on immediate skin-to-skin contact for very preterm infants and on resuscitation of newborns at birth. Her research uses randomised trials in Scandinavian neonatal intensive care units to examine thermoregulation, stress responses, mother–infant cortisol patterns and neurodevelopment up to two years. She also uses real-time observation, video analysis and dry-electrode ECG and pulse oximetry monitoring to document resuscitation practice and outcomes in a Norwegian hospital and in rural Tanzania.

name: Hans Morten Lossius
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Hans Morten Lossius researches prehospital emergency medicine, with a focus on helicopter and ground emergency medical services, airway management and paediatric emergencies. His work uses nationwide population-based cohort studies, multicentre observational studies, quasi-experimental educational evaluations and infrastructure mapping, drawing on data from Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Germany. Applications include clinical practice, EMS training and planning of emergency care access.

name: Hege Langli Ersdal
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Hege Langli Ersdal's publications cover newborn resuscitation and maternal and newborn care quality, mainly in Tanzania, Ethiopia and Norway, as well as stroke thrombectomy services and surgical training in Norway. Methods include randomized and stepped-wedge trials, prospective observational and video studies, registry analyses, facility surveys, cost-effectiveness analysis, qualitative interviews and international guideline reviews. Applications are simulation-based training, clinical guidelines, facility readiness, and health service delivery in low-resource and limited-volume settings.

name: Heidi Dombestein
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Heidi Dombestein studies resilience in healthcare and how adaptive capacity supports high-quality, safe care, mainly in Norwegian homecare, nursing homes and hospitals. Her work uses qualitative designs such as multiple case studies, focus groups, interviews, workshop observation and stakeholder analysis, alongside systematic, scoping and narrative reviews. Topics include risk perception among homecare leaders and professionals, management and champions, patient and family involvement, learning tools for putting resilience into practice, and patient and caregiver experiences in stroke and dementia care.

name: Helle Håve Stangeland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Helle Håve Stangeland studies long-term outcomes after ischemic stroke in working-age patients and the links between childhood trauma and later health in young people. Her stroke work uses MRI, deep-learning brain age estimation, lesion-symptom mapping and machine learning to examine brain aging, cognition, emotion recognition and return to work. Her epidemiological work links population survey data from the HUNT study with Norwegian national registries to examine psychiatric disorders, prescription analgesic use and alcohol problems, alongside trauma screening in chronic pain care.

name: Henrik Wethe Koch
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Henrik Wethe Koch studies the use of artificial intelligence in population-based mammography screening, using retrospective data from BreastScreen Norway. His work compares AI risk scores with radiologist double reading, examines performance by mammographic density, cancer location, prior screening rounds and false positives, and includes radiologist review and a survey of radiologists' expectations. He also analyses longitudinal changes in mammographic density in relation to breast cancer risk using mixed-effects regression.

name: Hilda Bø Lyng
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Hilda Bø Lyng studies resilience and adaptive capacity in healthcare, covering hospital teams, aged and long-term care, and a hospital supported by the Red Cross in Nigeria. Her work uses systematic reviews, document and policy analysis, cross-country comparison, qualitative case studies and survey development with psychometric validation, including the Resilience in Healthcare Capacities Assessment. It addresses healthcare leadership, workforce wellbeing and shortages, patient safety and incident reporting, and collaborative learning tools.

name: Ingrid Tjoflåt
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Ingrid Tjoflåt studies nursing and midwifery education, with a strong focus on simulation-based education in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly Malawi and Tanzania, and on training in postpartum hemorrhage management. Her work uses qualitative, mixed-methods, quasi-experimental, cross-sectional, Delphi and meta-synthesis designs to assess student learning, educator practices, debriefing and barriers to implementing simulation. She also examines virtual simulation for clinical judgment, non-technical skills assessment for operating room nurses, and postoperative nursing care in a conflict-affected hospital in Nigeria.

name: Ingvild Dalen
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Ingvild Dalen's publications apply biostatistical and epidemiological methods to clinical questions in Norway and abroad, including cohort and registry studies, survival and regression modelling, individual patient data meta-analysis, and randomized trials. Application areas include Parkinson's disease prognosis, dementia drug use, obstetrics and fetal Doppler ultrasound, paediatric bronchiolitis care, surgical and trauma outcomes, adrenal insufficiency, and arthroplasty outcome measures. Further work covers digital insomnia treatment for older adults, health assessment for older people living at home, and a stepped-wedge trial on reducing birth-related deaths in Tanzania.

name: Ingvild Margreta Morken
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Ingvild Margreta Morken studies nurse-assisted eHealth and remote patient monitoring for people with long-term illness, particularly heart failure and colorectal cancer, during the transition from hospital to home. Her work combines qualitative interview and longitudinal studies, mixed methods evaluation, literature reviews, and trial and feasibility protocols to examine self-management, self-care, usability, acceptability, nursing work and research recruitment. She has also carried out a study of point-of-care ultrasound performed by intensive care nurses in a cardiac unit.

name: Irene Hodnefjell Enge
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Irene Hodnefjell Enge studies simulation-based learning in health professions education, with a focus on collaborative and peer-to-peer simulation during clinical nursing placements. Her work uses pilot and focus group studies to explore how students learn and engage in practice settings, and includes developing a simulation method for use across health education programmes. She has also written on the role of gender in adolescent mental health.

name: Irene Rettedal Siren
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Siren Irene Rettedal studies newborn and preterm care, including immediate skin-to-skin contact and its effects on infant stress regulation, mother–infant cortisol synchrony and parental mental health, using randomised trials and systematic reviews. She also examines delivery-room resuscitation through observational studies, video and thermal recordings, dry-electrode ECG heart rate monitoring and AI-based video analysis, and contributes to international resuscitation guideline reviews. Further work covers neonatal care in Ethiopia and Tanzania, with facility readiness surveys, qualitative studies and an implementation trial protocol, and a neonatal intensive care unit case report of resistant bacterial infection.

name: Irene Sirevåg
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Irene Sirevåg researches operating room nursing, focusing on the non-technical skills (communication, teamwork, situation awareness, leadership and ethical accountability) that support patient safety in surgery. She uses Delphi panels, content validity indexing, thematic analysis and mixed-methods designs to develop and validate the NOTSORN behavioural marker tool, and her work extends to its use in nursing education. She also studies workforce retention, including a feasibility study of exoskeletons to reduce physical strain on operating room nurses, and educational resources such as a podcast for master's students.

name: Jeffrey Braithwaite
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Jeffrey Braithwaite's publications examine health system performance, patient safety and quality of care, using methods such as comparative policy and document analysis, systematic reviews, qualitative interviews, surveys, psychometric scale development and retrospective cohort analysis of linked administrative data. Topics include reform evaluation across countries, incident investigation and disclosure, resilience and systems leadership, disaster preparedness, and implementation of care pathways and clinical guidelines. Application settings include hospitals, aged care, oncology, paediatrics and maternal health, mainly in Australia.

name: Jicke Elon Gustaf Höök
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Jicke Höök studies how multiple professional teams coordinate across the stroke patient pathway, drawing on multiteam system theory and concept analysis. The work uses qualitative methods and multi-site, multi-professional observation, and also covers resilience in complex care pathways and person-centred practice, including a Swedish adaptation of a student inventory. The application domain is stroke care and healthcare teamwork, with projects connected to a Horizon Europe-funded initiative.

name: Jo Røislien
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Jo Røislien works on biostatistics and health data analysis, with a focus on prehospital and critical care, health communication and medical education. His publications use mathematical location optimization and geospatial modelling to plan helicopter ambulance bases and stroke units in Norway, and also include systematic and scoping reviews, randomized and quasi-experimental education studies, regression analyses of survey data, and qualitative interviews. Application areas include emergency medical services, acute stroke care, simulation and ultrasound training, pandemic and adolescent health messaging, and digital mental health for minority youth.

name: Karina Aase
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Karina Aase studies how health and social care services work in practice and how people experience them, using mainly qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups, observation, and journey mapping, along with scoping reviews, stakeholder analysis, service design workshops and mixed methods protocols. Her work covers supported housing for adults with intellectual disabilities, integrated and family-centred care for children with cerebral palsy, stroke care, home care for older people, and ambulance and prehospital services. Recurring themes include patient safety, professional adaptation, teamwork, coordination across services and the experiences of service users, families and frontline staff.

name: Karoline Lode-Kolz
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Karoline Lode-Kolz studies immediate skin-to-skin contact between parents and very preterm infants in neonatal intensive care, mainly through the IPISTOSS randomised clinical trial in Norway and Sweden. The work examines physiological outcomes (temperature control, cardiorespiratory stability), infant stress responses and cortisol, mother-infant interaction, parental depression and anxiety, and development up to two years, and also includes a systematic review of trials in high-resource settings. Methods include randomised trials, standardised behavioural and developmental assessments, salivary cortisol sampling and regression analyses.

name: Kristin Akerjordet
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Kristin Akerjordet studies resilience, mental well-being and leadership among health and aged care workers and informal caregivers, and develops digital educational resources and co-creation approaches in nursing education. Her work mainly uses systematic and scoping reviews, qualitative interviews and focus groups with thematic analysis, and a cross-country mixed-methods project to design a leadership toolbox. Application areas include elderly and nursing home care, nursing student stress and emotional intelligence, clinician emotion regulation, simulation feedback and contraceptive counselling in Tanzania.

name: Kristin Alstveit Laugaland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Kristin Alstveit Laugaland studies clinical education in nursing, focusing on first-year student nurses' placements in nursing homes and the roles of students, nurse educators and registered nurse mentors. Using qualitative methods such as focus groups, interviews, observation, video-stimulated recall and scoping review, the work examines supervision, assessment and mentorship practices. It also covers co-creation with stakeholders to design and evaluate digital educational resources that support placement learning.

name: Kristin Glenna Bodsberg
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Kristin Glenna Bodsberg conducts qualitative research in nursing, covering both cancer survivorship and nursing education. Using interviews and focus groups analysed with content analysis, her work examines how women with breast cancer prepare to return to work during treatment, and how nursing students and clinical nurses experience digital tools such as a clinical skills training app and student-made digital stories. She has also written on spiritual and existential care and on a digital simulation app for nursing students.

name: Kristin Tønsager
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Kristin Tønsager studies prehospital emergency medicine, focusing on out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and the care of injured patients before they reach hospital. Her work includes a multicentre randomised controlled trial across Norway, Denmark and Italy testing aortic balloon occlusion as an addition to advanced life support, and a prospective observational study of video streaming in emergency medical communication centres and its link to bystander first aid. The studies combine clinical trial and observational designs with regression analysis of outcomes such as return of spontaneous circulation and recognition of first aid needs.

name: Kristy Elizabeth Stohlmann
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Kristy Elizabeth Stohlmann studies how experienced nurses and other healthcare workers learn and adapt to new work practices, with a focus on workplace learning and professional development. Her work uses qualitative methods, including interviews analysed thematically, in Norwegian public healthcare settings, with ultrasound-guided peripheral venous cannulation as a main example. She also writes on pedagogical thinking and reflexive spaces as supports for resilience in healthcare practice.

name: Lars Vatne Jacobsen
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Lars Vatne Jacobsen studies medical education with a focus on teaching point-of-care ultrasound to health professionals. The publication compares remote, videoconference-guided ultrasound training with classroom teaching in a group of 44 prehospital critical care students, using pre- and post-course tests of knowledge, image interpretation, scanning technique and clinical decision-making. The work applies to telemedicine and training in settings that require physical distancing or are geographically remote.

name: Lene Schibevaag
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Lene Schibevaag studies resilience and adaptive capacity in healthcare as a multilevel phenomenon, spanning patients and families, frontline staff, managers, organizations and policymakers. Her work uses qualitative methods such as interviews, grounded theory, narrative meta-synthesis, stakeholder analysis and participatory workshops to build frameworks, learning tools and policy recommendations. Application areas include hospitals, nursing homes, home care, quality improvement implementation and safety investigation training in Norway.

name: Maha Kamran
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Maha Kamran studies the wellbeing of informal caregivers, such as family members, who support older people, using a cross-sectional study design. The work was presented at a joint symposium on resilience engineering and resilient health care, and its keywords point to a European setting and to patient safety. The publication provides limited detail, so the specific methods and findings are not described here.

name: Malin Emilia Rosell Magerøy
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Malin Emilia Rosell Magerøy studies how healthcare leaders in Norwegian nursing homes handle the combined duty of protecting staff health, safety and environment and ensuring patient safety and quality of care. Her work uses qualitative case studies, with interviews and focus groups involving politicians, senior leaders, mid-level managers and frontline department leaders, analysed through thematic and content analysis and linked to human factors and resilience frameworks such as SEIPS. She has also reviewed the literature on how full-time work culture and long shifts relate to quality and safety of care in primary healthcare.

name: Malin Knutsen Glette
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Malin Knutsen Glette studies resilience, leadership, patient safety and staff wellbeing in healthcare, with a focus on elderly care, nursing homes, home care and primary care. Her work combines systematic, scoping and meta-synthesis reviews with qualitative interview and focus group studies, and a mixed-methods project developing a digital toolbox for leaders. Application areas include pandemic response in rural services, palliative home care, care coordination across service interfaces, medication management and ambulatory surgery safety.

name: Marcus Thomas Thor Roalsø
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Marcus Thomas Thor Roalsø studies surgical outcomes and tumour biology in pancreatic and liver cancers, using national registry data, multicentre cohorts, systematic reviews and meta-analyses. His work examines recurrence, survival, sex differences, cachexia and neoadjuvant therapy after pancreatic resection, and repeat liver surgery for colorectal metastases. He also builds patient-derived organoid models from resected tumours to explore cancer metabolism, drug sensitivity and precision oncology in pancreatic and neuroendocrine cancers.

name: Maren Kristine Raknes Sogstad
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Maren Kristine Raknes Sogstad studies long-term care for older adults and for children with complex needs, focusing on how services are organised, allocated and experienced, mainly in Norway. Her work combines qualitative methods (interviews, focus groups, observation), register-based and survey analyses, systematic reviews, and cross-country comparisons of care systems. Topics include service allocation and needs assessment, informal carers, care-related quality of life measured with ASCOT, intermediate care, care workforce resilience, and integrated family-centred care for children with cerebral palsy.

name: Maria Camila Gonzalez Velez
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Maria C. Gonzalez studies dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson's disease and Parkinson's disease dementia, with a focus on biomarkers and disease progression. Her work uses multicenter cohort data, including plasma and cerebrospinal fluid markers, MRI measures, genetic variants and clinical assessments, analysed with longitudinal mixed-effects, survival and classification models. Applications include diagnosis, distinguishing Lewy body disease from Alzheimer's disease, prognosis of cognitive, motor and neuropsychiatric change, sex differences in brain atrophy, and the design of clinical trials.

name: Maria Nyre Vigmostad
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Maria Nyre Vigmostad works on clinical research in urological cancers, with a focus on prostate cancer diagnosis and treatment and on metastatic spread in renal cell carcinoma. Her publications include a cost analysis using Markov modelling, a real-world study of biopsy decisions guided by the Stockholm3 blood test and MRI, a protocol for a multinational randomised trial of curative versus conservative therapy in men aged 75 and over, and a review of pancreatic metastasis from kidney cancer. The work spans health economics, diagnostic strategy, geriatric oncology and cancer biology.

name: Marius Rehn
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Marius Rehn works in prehospital and emergency medicine, covering cardiac arrest, trauma, haemorrhagic shock and acute stroke care. His work combines randomised and retrospective clinical studies, animal experiments, physiological monitoring studies, geospatial optimisation modelling, systematic and narrative reviews, and clinical practice guidelines. Application areas include helicopter and air ambulance services, dispatcher-assisted first aid, neonatal transport, intensive care, and care of casualties in conflict and civil unrest.

name: Matthew Robert Hilditch
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Matthew Robert Hilditch's work centres on paramedic and prehospital emergency care, including training for critical care paramedics in aviation-based emergency medical services and the recognition of stroke by ambulance crews. He uses systematic reviews to compare evidence on simulation-based education and on the FAST and BE-FAST screening tools. He also writes case-based clinical reports on managing COPD and suspected meningococcal disease, covering guideline-led prescribing and the role of non-medical prescribers.

name: Melissa Anne Elin Authen Weibell
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Melissa Anne Elin Authen Weibell studies psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, combining clinical research on recovery, cognition, early intervention and antipsychotic treatment with biological work on immune and inflammatory markers and epigenetics. Her methods include Delphi consensus studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, plasma biomarker comparisons in large patient and control cohorts, gene expression analyses and DNA methylation association studies using birth registry data. The work applies to psychosis care and research, including standardising recovery outcomes, understanding long-term cognitive trajectories and identifying biological mechanisms of severe mental illness.

name: Melissa Auten Weibell
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Melissa Auten Weibell studies the role of innate immune activity in severe mental illnesses, particularly schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Using a large patient and healthy-control cohort, her work measures blood levels of IL-18 system proteins, inflammasome-related gene expression and lipid markers, and examines how cholesterol patterns relate to inflammation. The research aims to clarify inflammatory mechanisms in psychotic disorders and point to possible therapeutic targets.

name: Nils Petter Oveland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Nils Petter Oveland works on point-of-care ultrasound and other bedside diagnostics for emergency and critical care, including consensus-based clinical recommendations for lung ultrasound and studies of ultrasound teaching. His research also covers experimental work in pigs, such as testing a microwave device to detect air and blood in the chest after trauma, and a report on fatal sepsis traced to contaminated propofol anaesthesia. Application areas include prehospital and emergency medicine, trauma care, telemedicine education and anaesthesia safety.

name: Nina Hjertvikrem
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Nina Hjertvikrem studies cardiac rehabilitation for people with coronary artery disease, with a focus on designing and developing a digital rehabilitation program (eCardiacRehab). Her design work uses co-creation with clinicians, developers and patients, including workshops, personas, think-aloud usability testing and qualitative content analysis. She also analyses large multicentre cohorts of patients after percutaneous coronary intervention, examining gender differences in risk factors, anxiety and depression, health literacy, quality of life, and the use of follow-up services.

name: Nina Vatland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Nina Vatland's work covers two areas: independent safety investigation in Norway, viewed through a risk management lens with a focus on the Norwegian Safety Investigation Authority (UKOM), and educational practice in higher education. Her teaching-related publications look at interdisciplinary simulation, simulation in paramedic education, and the Cognita model of group and activity-based learning. Her work applies to public safety and accident investigation as well as health and emergency care education.

name: Olav Røise
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Olav Røise's research centres on trauma care and injury epidemiology, particularly traumatic brain injury, using national registry linkages, prospective cohorts, machine learning, Mendelian randomization and systematic review. Studies cover trauma registry development and triage prediction, long-term outcomes such as disability, work absence, rehabilitation pathways and opioid use after injury, and injuries from cycling, micromobility and martial arts. He also uses qualitative interviews to examine clinical decision-making and healthcare resilience in hospital transfer, pain management, home care and nursing home settings.

name: Paul Magnus Heggland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology

name: Pegah Sedgh
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Pegah Sedgh studies how leadership can support the mental wellbeing and resilience of health and care workers, with a focus on elderly care and Norwegian home care services. Her work includes a literature review and a mixed-methods study of leadership, and she also reflects on the use of reflexive thematic analysis in doctoral research. The findings are relevant for care organisations and managers seeking to improve the work-related wellbeing of their staff.

name: Per Kristian Hyldmo
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Per Kristian Hyldmo studies emergency and prehospital care, with a strong focus on acute stroke treatment access and outcomes. His work uses registry-based observational studies, before-after training studies, systematic and scoping reviews, and phantom-based imaging experiments. Application areas include thrombectomy services in low-volume and remote regions, simulation and tele-ultrasound education, prehospital pain management, aeromedical retrieval, and trauma immobilization during radiography.

name: Petter Viksveen
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Petter Viksveen studies mental health services and community care in Norway, with a focus on adolescents and youth from refugee, asylum-seeker, minority and Indigenous backgrounds, and on home care for older adults. His work relies mainly on qualitative interviews, workshops, co-design and systematic reviews, along with mixed-methods project protocols, and draws on the views of youth, parents, health professionals and other stakeholders. It addresses cultural sensitivity, trust, user involvement and shared decision-making, and it extends to digital mental health services and resilience among older adult care workers.

name: Philipp Seidel
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Philipp Seidel works in critical care and emergency medicine, focusing on adults who survive cardiac arrest or are in septic shock. His publications cover large international randomized trials and their protocols and analysis plans, testing sedation depth, fever management, blood pressure targets and intravenous fluid restriction, along with substudies on kidney outcomes and early neurological prognosis using CT, EEG and blood markers. He has also tested microwave sensing in a pig model as a point-of-care method for detecting air and blood in the chest after trauma.

name: Ragnhild Margrete Finnesand Michaelsen
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Ragnhild Margrete Finnesand Michaelsen studies how life stories are used as a tool in professional elderly care, with a focus on nursing homes. Her work in an interdisciplinary project combines a survey of the documentation forms used in nursing homes in a region of western Norway with a comparative close reading of their style and modes of communication. It examines how practical and relational purposes become mixed in these tools.

name: Runar Salte
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Runar Salte's listed work examines traumatic pneumothorax in civilian and military injury settings, separating simple pneumothorax from tension pneumothorax and comparing patients who breathe on their own with those on positive pressure ventilation. The publication is a position-style review that sets out definitions, pathophysiology, diagnosis and a standardized nomenclature. It also proposes treatment approaches that differ according to ventilation status, with relevance to emergency and trauma care.

name: Silje Karin Sjøseth Askeland
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Silje Karin Sjøseth Askeland studies how long-term services for children with cerebral palsy and their families are organised, coordinated and experienced, with a focus on family-centred and integrated care. Using qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups, observation of multidisciplinary meetings, document review, stakeholder analysis and thematic analysis, her work examines the roles of service providers across health, education and welfare sectors, how providers adapt their practice, and the strategies families use to navigate services. The work applies a resilience perspective to collaboration between families and providers in paediatric care.

name: Sina Furnes Øyri
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Sina Furnes Øyri studies how external regulation, inspection and investigation shape quality, safety and resilience in healthcare and other public services in Norway. Using qualitative interviews, document analysis and meta-synthesis, her work examines the views of inspectors, surgeons and child welfare and Nav staff on supervision, adverse event reporting and improvement work after regulatory findings. It also includes comparisons of Norwegian and US external evaluation systems and commissioned reports for the Norwegian Board of Health Supervision.

name: Siri Lerstøl Olsen
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Siri Lerstøl Olsen studies patient safety and care of deteriorating and older hospital patients, with a focus on rapid response systems and on delirium in emergency departments. Her work combines qualitative methods (focus groups, interviews, in situ simulation, framework-based analysis of adaptations), a mortality review of surgical ward patients, and a scoping review of the delirium literature. The studies address how early warning systems are implemented, modified and experienced in Norwegian hospitals, and where evidence on detection and prevention is lacking.

name: Siri Wiig
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Siri Wiig studies resilience, patient safety and quality of care across health and aged care systems, treating them as multilevel systems spanning teams, organisations and national policy. Her work uses qualitative studies, systematic and scoping reviews, comparative policy analysis and survey instrument development and validation. It addresses workforce shortages, staff mental wellbeing, leadership, digital health workarounds and the evaluation of health reforms in home care, long-term care and hospitals.

name: Sissel Iren Eikeland Husebø
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: S. E. Husebø studies nursing education, with a focus on simulation-based learning, debriefing, facilitator and operator roles, clinical judgment and the teaching of practical nursing skills in simulation centres and clinical placements across Scandinavia. The work uses surveys, focus groups and interviews, quasi-experimental comparisons and scoping reviews. It also addresses clinical practice topics, including interprofessional team training and patient safety on surgical wards, person-centred stroke care, recovery and coping among cancer patients, surgical patient safety measurement and telemedicine for chronic wound care.

name: Siv Hilde Berg
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Siv Hilde Berg studies mental health care, suicide prevention and patient safety, with attention to trust, psychological safety and resilient performance among patients and professionals. She also works on health and risk communication, public trust in government during crises, and adolescent and minority youth involvement in mental health services and digital services. Her methods include systematic and scoping reviews, qualitative and mixed methods studies, cohort and randomized experiments, and analysis of repeated survey data.

name: Soffien Chadli Ajmi
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Soffien Chadli Ajmi studies acute stroke care, focusing on how quickly and accurately patients are recognised and treated from emergency dispatch through hospital thrombolysis and thrombectomy. The work uses cohort studies, registry analyses, national surveys, pre-post interventions and cost-effectiveness analysis to examine stroke mimics, dizziness presentations, regional differences in care and functional outcomes. It also evaluates multidisciplinary simulation training and quality improvement projects as ways to shorten treatment times and improve patient outcomes.

name: Solveig Hodne
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Solveig Hodne studies health law and patient rights, including nationwide analyses of malpractice and compensation claims in Norway for pancreatic cancer and acute pancreatitis, looking at claim rates, causes such as diagnostic delay, outcomes and payouts. She also works on the InvolveMENT mixed methods project, which uses cohort surveys, interviews and a randomized trial to improve digital mental health services for national minority, Indigenous (Sámi) and refugee youth, and examines equity of access through a human rights lens. Her work further touches on legal skills in nursing, social work and child welfare education and on involving relatives in nursing education.

name: Stephen Johan Mikal Sollid
department: Department of Quality and Health Technology
summary: Stephen Johan Mikal Sollid studies prehospital and emergency medical services, covering patient safety, quality measurement and trauma care in ambulance and helicopter services.
