He also contributes to Parkinson's disease research, including an online trial of video-based cognitive behavioural therapy for depression, a survey of cannabis use, and a study of cognitive decline.

name: Aleksandra Sevic
summary: Aleksandra Sevic studies digital stress (technostress) among employees, including how it is measured, what predicts it and how it relates to emotional exhaustion and burnout, particularly in Norwegian workplaces and higher education. Her work uses survey-based methods such as scale translation and validation, factor analysis and hierarchical regression, and also covers public attitudes toward and acceptance of artificial intelligence in relation to personality, age, gender and application context. She has additionally carried out systematic reviews and meta-analyses on workplace eHealth interventions and on alcohol use and sickness absence, and has worked on a virtual reality intervention for technostress.

name: Ayo Zahra
summary: Ayo Zahra develops and validates open-source image analysis tools for measuring brain volumes from ultra-low-field MRI in infants and toddlers. The work uses age-specific templates and priors for automated segmentation, compares results against high-field MRI with correlation and percentage-error measures, and applies mixed-effects models to examine age, sex and birthweight. The application focus is accessible infant neuroimaging in low- and middle-income settings, with cohorts in South Africa and Uganda.

name: Bianka Anna Karshikoff
summary: Bianka Anna Karshikoff studies how low-grade and acute inflammation relate to pain, mood, anxiety, sleep and sickness behavior. Her work combines blood cytokine and multiplex protein panels, questionnaires and validation analyses, brain imaging, and experimental endotoxin challenges in healthy volunteers, as well as natural inflammation in seasonal allergy. Application areas include chronic pain and pelvic pain, psychological comorbidity, response to behavioral treatment, and odor-based cues of illness.

name: Danilo Garcia
summary: Danilo Garcia studies personality, well-being and mental health, often using Cloninger's biopsychosocial model, across student, clinical, older-adult and community populations. His work uses surveys, structural equation modeling, network analysis, psychometric validation and literature or policy reviews, and increasingly applies AI and language models to mental health assessment and therapy outcomes. Application areas include education, health-care training, physical activity and aging, school health, media psychology and sustainable food systems.

name: Erik Lerdahl
summary: Erik Lerdahl is represented by a 2025 piece in Norwegian on music, silence and creativity, built around a conversation with Alexander Refsum Jensenius, who stood still for ten minutes each day for a year. The work looks at how sounds and sensory impressions in our surroundings affect people, drawing on research on rhythm, time and movement. It considers what music and stillness mean for personal wellbeing and creative activity.

name: Francesco Margoni
summary: Francesco Margoni studies how moral reasoning, cooperation, fairness and ideas about leadership and authority develop from infancy through old age. His work uses looking-time experiments with infants and toddlers, child and adult behavioural tasks and surveys across several countries, and also covers research methods such as the violation-of-expectation paradigm and subjective logic. Applications include human-robot interaction and ethical decision-making among intelligence professionals.

name: Jens Hetland
summary: Jens Hetland works on cognitive functioning and emotional functioning in people with substance use disorders, including difficulties such as executive problems and anhedonia during recovery from polysubstance use. His publications combine clinical and research expertise with literature review to propose a tiered model for assessing cognition in specialist addiction treatment in Norway. The work is aimed at clinical psychology practice and at improving treatment planning and follow-up for patients.

name: Jone Ravndal Bjørnestad
summary: Jone Ravndal Bjørnestad studies mental health and substance use recovery alongside consumer behavior in banking. Work on psychosis risk, substance use disorders and contraceptive prescribing draws on systematic reviews and meta-analyses, qualitative interviews and focus groups, and longitudinal modelling such as latent class and dynamic structural equation models. Work on banking uses representative survey and longitudinal data with regression and moderated mediation analyses to examine how satisfaction and self-efficacy relate to bank-switching intention and behavior. Further work covers a gaming-based intervention for unemployed young adults and training for foster care counselors.

name: Lilla Magyari
summary: Lilla Magyari studies how brains and behavior support language and communication, using EEG and event-related potential recordings alongside behavioral experiments. Her work compares humans with dogs and pigs to examine neural responses to vocalizations and to object words, and also looks at speech prosody in multi-talker listening, turn-taking prediction in conversation, and pronoun use in political speech. She additionally conducts reading research, including experiments on screen versus print comprehension in vocational students, comparisons of reading tests for struggling readers, and work on author recognition tests and literary reading.

name: Liv Sand
summary: Liv Sand studies eating disorders and their overlap with personality disorders and perfectionism, and the links between childhood and adolescent trauma and mental health outcomes. Her work combines clinical case studies and commentary on integrated, CBT-based treatment with large Norwegian population surveys and national patient registry data, analysed using logistic regression and latent class analysis. Application areas include psychotherapy for comorbid conditions, depression risk among university students, and use of child and adolescent mental health services.

name: Marita Kallesten Brønnick
summary: Marita Kallesten Brønnick studies how hormonal contraceptives, especially the intrauterine system, are prescribed to adolescents and how this relates to mental health outcomes such as depression. Her work uses focus group interviews with healthcare professionals at Norwegian health centers, analysed thematically, to identify who is recommended which products and why. The findings are intended to help future quantitative studies account for selective prescribing as a source of confounding.

name: Muriel Marisa Katharina Bruchhage
summary: Muriel Marisa Katharina Bruchhage studies early brain development in infants and children, mainly using structural, functional and diffusion MRI, including portable ultra-low-field scanners for low- and middle-income settings. Her publications cover automated morphometry pipelines, normative and longitudinal statistical models of brain growth, and how maternal education, maternal BMI, FTO genotype, nutrition and the gut microbiome relate to brain structure, connectivity, myelination and cognition. She has also contributed work on the cerebellum in ageing and cerebellar connectivity, and an animal MRI study of frontostriatal circuits in compulsive behaviour.

name: Nicolay Gausel
summary: Nicolay Gausel studies moral emotions, especially shame, and how they shape defensive or repair-oriented responses in close relationships, in social groups and around prejudice toward immigrants. His work combines conversation analysis of research interviews with young people who have committed sexual violations, experiments with university students, and psychometric testing of a therapy outcome-monitoring scale on a sample of Norwegian clients. Applications include social work practice, psychotherapy measurement and understanding social mobilization against prejudice.

name: Pravin Tembjerg
summary: Pravin Tembjerg studies family separation and reunification, child welfare and mental health services, drawing on theoretical analysis, qualitative interviews, quantitative comparisons and national cohort data. Publications cover child protection, foster care training, family group conferences, attachment and children's mental health, as well as carer involvement in recovery-oriented services such as assertive community treatment in Norway. Work also includes a national cohort study of parent mortality after a child's death.

name: Synne Wiberg
summary: Synne Wiberg studies how digitalization affects the psychosocial well-being and safety of workers in Norway's offshore petroleum industry. Her work combines in-depth interviews with offshore personnel and a narrative review of government and industry reports to examine how workers use digital tools such as handheld devices and how psychosocial factors are treated in industry documents. The research relates to high-risk workplaces and to balancing efficiency gains with worker well-being and safety.

name: Tore Tjora
summary: Tore Tjora studies behavior, mental health and work-related outcomes in Norwegian populations using surveys, registry data, longitudinal designs and psychometric validation. His work covers consumer bank-switching and self-efficacy, adolescent emotion regulation and adversity, psychosis risk and substance use, and safety climate and work disability in the petroleum and welfare sectors. Methods include regression, structural equation and latent class or growth models, decision-tree machine learning, and qualitative focus groups.

name: Vendela Husberg-Bru
summary: Vendela Husberg-Bru studies hazardous alcohol use in middle-aged and older adults, using population-based survey data from the Tromsø Study in Norway. Her cross-sectional analyses, using chi-square tests, analysis of covariance and logistic regression, examine how hazardous drinking relates to health behaviours, health-related quality of life and past potentially traumatic events. She has also examined alcohol use after the transition to retirement, with a public health focus on ageing populations.

name: Wenche Ten Velden Hegelstad
summary: Wenche Ten Velden Hegelstad studies early psychosis, covering first-episode psychosis, clinical high risk states and long-term recovery, using large international neuroimaging consortium data alongside longitudinal cohort follow-up, registry linkage, trajectory modelling, psychometric validation and systematic review. Her work also includes qualitative interview studies of recovery, help-seeking, service use and virtual reality therapy, and covers suicidality, childhood adversity, antipsychotic treatment response and family psychoeducation. Applications lie in early detection, mental health service delivery, and standardising recovery definitions and outcomes in psychosis research.

name: Aleksandar Bozic
summary: Aleksandar Bozic studies social work and social services, with a focus on social innovation, civil society organisations and NGOs, and services for children, families and migrants. His work uses qualitative methods such as interviews, document and policy analysis, scoping reviews and social network analysis, covering topics like Family Group Conferences, school bullying and religious diversity, psychosocial care for children in transnational families, and international field placements in social work education. It also includes applied research with a Norwegian municipality on coordinated public services.

name: Anne Ingeborg Apeland Svalastog
summary: Anne Ingeborg Apeland Svalastog studies child welfare and social work, with a main focus on kinship foster care in Norway and how foster carers and adolescents experience contact with Child Welfare Services. She uses qualitative interviews, a qualitative evidence synthesis and mixed-methods surveys, drawing on sociological theory such as ambivalence and sense of coherence. Her work also covers youth social exclusion and cooperation between public and voluntary sectors in municipalities, as well as work-integrated learning in child welfare education.

name: Anne Katrine Folkman
summary: Anne Katrine Folkman researches social work and child welfare education in Norway, with a focus on work-integrated learning (WIL), student agency and the development of professional skills for practice. She also studies co-production and interprofessional collaboration in child welfare services, family reunification and schools, as well as teachers' experiences of online schooling. Her methods include surveys, interviews, observations, thematic analysis, mixed-methods designs and narrative reviews.

name: Ayan Abdi Mohamoud Handulle
summary: Ayan Abdi Mohamoud Handulle studies how Somali and other ethnic minority migrants in Norway experience stigma, racialization, Islamophobia and fear of child welfare services, using ethnography and in-depth interviews interpreted mainly through Goffman's interaction order and stigma theory. Her work also covers transnational family life and return migration, migrant parents separated from children, and refugee grief support through an action research project with municipalities. She additionally contributes to international and comparative social work education, including partnerships between Norwegian universities and institutions in Africa and Cuba.

name: Brita Gjerstad
summary: Brita Gjerstad studies how welfare technology and digital care are developed, governed and experienced in Norwegian primary healthcare, drawing on care ethics and co-creation frameworks. Her work relies mainly on qualitative interviews, discourse and thematic analysis, action research and a scoping review, with participants including healthcare professionals, managers, technology suppliers and relatives of nursing home residents. She also works on municipal housing and welfare planning, including technology in housing for residents with severe substance use and mental health disorders, municipal governance of acute care units, and help seeking for couple-relationship problems.

name: Britt Ingunn Misund
summary: Britt Ingunn Misund studies how Norwegian authorities organise and steer child protection services, focusing on the division of tasks between state and municipal levels. Using qualitative thematic analysis of public documents and evaluations, her work examines reforms, standardisation, legal and guidance-based steering, and the tension between national control and local discretion. Topics include equitable services, legal protection for children and the bureaucratisation of municipal child welfare.

name: Cornel Maria Nesseler
summary: Cornel Maria Nesseler studies discrimination, bias and performance in sport, esports and welfare settings. His methods include large-scale field and correspondence experiments using native- and foreign-sounding names, survey and video-based experiments, regression discontinuity designs and regression analysis, including causal random forests. Application areas include amateur and professional football, tennis coaching, esports, social work and welfare administration, and consumer behavior in the video game industry.

name: Eden Begna Gobena
summary: Eden Begna Gobena studies the experiences of women and mothers after imprisonment, mainly in Ethiopia, using descriptive phenomenological interviews, a qualitative systematic review and reflective fieldwork. The work covers stigma, poverty, mother-child bonds and reintegration, and draws out implications for social work practice, non-custodial sentencing and culturally sensitive support programmes. She also writes on decolonizing research methods and researcher training, and on researcher positionality and racialised experience in Nordic and teacher education settings.

name: Elisabeth Enoksen
summary: Elisabeth Enoksen studies social inclusion, child welfare and youth experiences in Norway, using mostly qualitative methods such as interviews and diary analysis, alongside surveys and co-creation approaches. Her work covers cross-sector collaboration between municipalities and voluntary organisations to prevent youth exclusion, support for parents with collaboration difficulties after separation, and belonging and social control among youth with cross-cultural upbringings. She has also examined survivors of institutional abuse applying for redress, children's lockdown experiences, Sámi nature-based education and international students' experiences.

name: Evelyn Sandøy Ottesen
summary: Evelyn Sandøy Ottesen studies social work education in Norway, with a focus on how work-integrated education and learning can build student agency and professional development. Her work includes a narrative critical review and also considers how relevant social work is in the workforce, including its role in elderly care and its potential to bring innovation to welfare services. The publications address how professionalism is taught and learned in higher education and how programmes connect to working life.

name: Heidi Lie Eriksen
summary: Heidi Lie Eriksen studies social work education and practice in Norway, with a focus on practice placements, supervision, student agency, and international field placements. She also researches frontline welfare work, including discretion in Nav offices and discrimination in welfare responses tested through a field experiment, as well as community and voluntary-sector collaboration to prevent youth exclusion. Her methods are mostly qualitative (interviews, observation, thematic and content analysis, surveys, narrative review) alongside experimental designs, and her work also touches on professional ethics and social work in healthcare.

name: Hulda Mjøll Gunnarsdottir
summary: Hulda Mjøll Gunnarsdottir studies social work and child welfare in Norway, including kinship and out-of-home care, young people's identities and relationships with child welfare services, and parental cooperation after family breakdown. She also examines social workers' working conditions, resilience, job satisfaction and emotional labour in settings such as criminal justice, outreach work, substance use treatment in residential care and violent extremism prevention. Her methods include interviews, narrative and thematic analysis, surveys with regression analysis, mixed-methods designs, qualitative evidence synthesis and collaborative development projects with municipalities.

name: Håvard Haugstvedt
summary: Håvard Haugstvedt studies social work and security topics, including outreach youth work, criminal justice social work, and multiagency prevention of radicalization and violent extremism in the Nordic countries. He uses interviews, focus groups, surveys and regression analyses, and also builds datasets of open-source incidents to examine how violent non-state actors and cartels use armed drones. His work applies to youth substance use prevention, social worker wellbeing and resilience during COVID-19, youth mental health and support for violence, and counterterrorism and security policy.

name: Ida Bruheim-Escobar
summary: Ida Bruheim-Escobar studies how digital technologies are used in social work, including their effects on communication, documentation, decision-making and relationships between clients and social workers. Her work uses an umbrella review method to synthesise findings from 24 systematic reviews across areas such as child welfare, mental health, migration and elderly care. She draws on sociotechnical systems theory and ethics of care to examine ethical concerns, digital inequalities and the limited inclusion of service-user perspectives.

name: Ingrid Djuvik Overskeid
summary: Ingrid Djuvik Overskeid studies child welfare in Norway, focusing on the Dialogue Process, a mediation-style approach offered by the Child Welfare Tribunal, and how it affects user involvement for children, parents and child welfare workers. Her PhD research is qualitative, drawing on focus group interviews with child welfare workers about decision-making and professional identity in complex cases involving alternative care. She has also shared this work at international seminars and conferences and taken part in international social work exchange with Cuba and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

name: Ingunn Studsrød
summary: Ingunn Studsrød studies social work and family issues, including domestic violence and post-separation abuse, child welfare services and support for parents after children are taken into care, and the experiences of marginalised groups such as young women in out-of-home care, survivors of institutional abuse and incarcerated mothers in Ethiopia. Her work relies mainly on qualitative interviews with thematic, narrative and phenomenological analysis, alongside national surveys, document analysis and cross-country comparison between Norway, Poland and Ethiopia. The publications address social work practice, public service design, help seeking and decolonial approaches to research.

name: Ingunn Tollisen Ellingsen
summary: Ingunn Tollisen Ellingsen studies child welfare and social work, with a main focus on family reunification and support for parents after out-of-home placement in Norway. She uses qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups, document analysis, narrative thematic analysis, Q methodology and literature reviews to examine the perspectives of professionals, foster parents, parents, young people and kinship carers. Her work also covers standardised assessment tools in decision-making, adolescent substance use, and municipal evaluations of citizen panels, coordinated services and voluntary-sector inclusion projects.

name: Ingunn Øyre
summary: Ingunn Øyre's work, as shown by a single 2026 publication, concerns quality in higher education, with a focus on the scope for action within special suitability assessment (særskilt skikkethetsvurdering). This is the process used in Norwegian professional programmes to judge whether students are suitable for their intended profession. The publication points to an interest in educational policy and practice in professional education, and no specific methods are indicated by the title alone.

name: Ismail Seçer
summary: Ismail Seçer studies trauma and mental health in children, adolescents and adults, especially survivors of the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, as well as school attendance problems and burnout among students and healthcare workers. His work combines psychometric scale adaptation, structural equation modelling, network analysis, latent profile analysis and meta-analysis with pilot intervention trials of a parent-child therapy adapted for disaster-related trauma. Application areas include clinical assessment, school-based prevention, cross-cultural comparison and disaster response.

name: Jan Otto Jacobsen
summary: Jan Otto Jacobsen studies how operational organisations such as the armed forces, police and emergency preparedness services learn from experience and turn it into shared knowledge. His work draws on organisational learning theory and case examples from the air force, police and the First World War, and examines barriers to learning, cultural change and structured debriefing methods such as After Action Review. He also addresses mission-based leadership, in which personnel are expected to exercise independent judgement.

name: Joakim Finne
summary: Joakim Finne studies how child welfare interventions are delivered in practice, with a focus on preventing child maltreatment in families with complex support needs. His work evaluates the implementation fidelity of a home-visiting programme called Family Partner, combining descriptive analysis of practitioner-reported routine data with thematic analysis of interviews and focus groups. The research informs how pilot trials and measures for complex public health and family support interventions are designed before full-scale randomized trials.

name: Kathrine Skoland
summary: Kathrine Skoland studies domestic and partner violence, child physical abuse and help seeking for couple-relationship problems, with a focus on Norway and comparisons with Poland. Her work uses population and youth surveys, focus groups with professionals, and comparative analysis to examine attitudes to gender equality and violence, disclosure by teenagers, perceived access to services, and cross-sector collaboration in prevention. She also contributes applied regional work on keeping skilled newcomers in Agder through social inclusion measures.

name: Kolbjørn Kallesten Brønnick
summary: Kolbjørn Kallesten Brønnick studies how psychological and cognitive factors shape behavior and health across several domains, including self-efficacy and bank-switching in Norwegian consumers, digital stress among employees, and cognitive function in people with brain metastases or neurodegenerative disease. His methods include representative surveys, longitudinal and regression analyses, scale development and validation, qualitative case studies, and EEG signal analysis with data harmonization and machine learning. Application areas include banking and consumer policy, workplace wellbeing, health communication, digital healthcare, mental health peer support and clinical neuropsychology.

name: Kristina Johansen
summary: Kristina Johansen conducts qualitative research in Norway on the psychosocial well-being, resilience and participation of unaccompanied minor and young refugees, drawing on recognition theory and a strengths perspective. Her methods include interviews, participant observation, participatory workshops and dialogue cafes, and she also examines family separation and reunification, grief and grief support among refugees, and research ethics with children and young people. The work is aimed at social work practice, welfare services and asylum and migration policy.

name: Liv Jorunn Baggegård Skippervik
summary: Liv Jorunn Baggegård Skippervik studies welfare law and legal practice in Norway, with a focus on the Nav administration and how frontline staff use discretion, negotiation and non-discrimination rules in their work. She combines legal analysis with social work perspectives in statutory commentaries, a textbook, an error review of legal application in Nav and work on legal skills in professional education. She has also examined dialogue-based and restorative approaches to reunification in child welfare cases and the role of professional judgement versus technical solutions such as AI.

name: Maren Sagvaag Retland
summary: Maren Sagvaag Retland studies intimate partner violence that continues after separation, with a focus on how families and welfare services handle custody, visitation and family reunification in Norway. Her work uses qualitative methods such as reflective thematic analysis of interviews with mothers about mandatory family mediation, along with literature review and discussion of legal issues. She also examines how legal application skills are understood in nursing, social work and child welfare education.

name: Marina Snipsøyr Sletten
summary: Marina Snipsøyr Sletten studies how child welfare services are governed at the municipal level in Norway. Her 2025 publication examines local political ownership of child welfare and draws on the experiences of municipal chief executives and child welfare leaders in working together with local politicians. The work falls within public administration and social welfare policy, with a focus on cooperation between political and administrative leadership.

name: Marita Wassbakk
summary: Marita Wassbakk studies the working conditions and professional experiences of staff in criminal justice and correctional services, including social workers and prison officers. Her work uses a mixed-methods survey of Norwegian criminal justice social workers, analysed with the job demands-resources model, to examine how COVID-19 infection control affected workload, collegial contact and service to users. She has also carried out a scoping review of the emotional expectations placed on prison officers.

name: Marte Tonning Otterlei
summary: Marte Tonning Otterlei studies child protection in Norway, focusing on care orders, child removals and family reunification. Using qualitative interviews analysed thematically and through positioning theory, her work examines the experiences of parents, child welfare workers and lawyers, including grief, stigma, legal rights and the stress of delivering bad news. She also researches dialogue-based decision-making such as dialogue conferences and dialogue processes, and writes on worker safety, children's participation and social work education.

name: Mikhail Gradovski
summary: Mikhail Gradovski studies education and social science through a dialogic lens, drawing on Bakhtin's ideas of dialogue and on methodological work on merged methods. His publications cover democratic schools in Norway and Sweden, analysis of kindergarten teacher education textbooks across the Norway-Russia border, and qualitative studies of student resistance in practice supervision for social work students. He also writes on supervision, leadership development through digital dialogue, doctoral education and PhD candidate surveys, and academic freedom.

name: Mira Aurora Marlow
summary: Mira Aurora Marlow studies the experiences of young women with a history in out-of-home and residential care, mainly in Norway, using narrative interviews and analysis informed by intersectional and feminist perspectives. Her work examines identity, visibility, agency, resistance to dominant stereotypes, wellbeing and participation in child welfare institutions, including how Norway's new Child Welfare Act relates to children's rights. She also addresses ethical questions of protection and participation in research with children and young people, with implications for social work practice and service user involvement.

name: Morten Tønnessen
summary: Morten Tønnessen works across biosemiotics, environmental humanities and cross-cultural psychology. His publications develop Uexküllian umwelt theory, ecosemiotics and phenomenological methods for studying human and animal experience, and apply them to the environmental crisis, animal welfare, nature philosophy and the ethics of Mars settlement. He also contributes to large multi-country survey studies on perceived inequality, well-being, power, status and love, and to qualitative interview research on outdoor recreation (friluftsliv) in youth residential care in Norway.

name: Nafiseh Kananifar
summary: Nafiseh Kananifar studies how personality traits relate to mental health, well-being and behavior in university students, healthcare workers, people with disabilities and people in addiction treatment. Her work uses questionnaire-based surveys analyzed with structural equation modeling, correlation and regression, as well as a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design to assess cognitive-behavioral training. Application areas include student mental health, occupational health and work addiction among nurses, rehabilitation, and addiction treatment.

name: Nina Thorbjørnsen
summary: Nina Thorbjørnsen studies social housing for people with severe co-occurring substance use and mental health disorders (ROP), with a focus on municipal care housing in Karmøy. Her work uses action research and qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups, workshops and site visits to examine user involvement and the choice of heating, ventilation and safety solutions. She also writes on quality development in social work education and on the role of social workers in elderly care.

name: Olga V Lehmann O
summary: Olga V Lehmann studies silence, emotion and meaning-making in psychology, using qualitative approaches such as content analysis, reflexive and developmentally oriented thematic analysis, case studies, and poetic and narrative methods. Her work also covers grief and bereavement, including online therapeutic writing for bereaved parents and fathers and frameworks for family separation and reunification in child protection. Further projects adapt an emotion-focused parenting program to an online, culturally inclusive format and examine writing among older adults in Norway.

name: Reidun Ims
summary: Reidun Ims studies how work and integration are linked for immigrants in the Norwegian welfare state, with attention to what this means for social work practice. Her research combines an integrative literature review of Norwegian studies with qualitative interviews analysed through interpretative phenomenological analysis, covering labour market outcomes, discrimination, immigrant women's workforce participation and immigrants' own experiences of control, exclusion and belonging. The work applies to integration policy, employment support services and social work education.

name: Richard Michael Piech
summary: Richard Michael Piech studies family relationships and wellbeing of children, young people and adults, using qualitative methods such as semi-structured and in-depth interviews analysed thematically. His work covers sibling relationships after parental divorce or placement in care, young carers in Ghana, and women diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood in Norway. The publications draw out implications for social workers and other professionals, including support for young carers and cooperation between health and child welfare services.

name: Sarah Catherine Patricia Duff Hean
summary: Sarah Catherine Patricia Duff Hean conducts mainly qualitative research in social work and child and family welfare, including sibling relationships after parental divorce, children's experiences of child protection services, and the inclusion of children with disabilities. Her work also covers criminal justice and rehabilitation (drug court participants, probation supervision, mothers after incarceration), unaccompanied refugee youth, and decolonial approaches to research training, using interviews, focus groups, phenomenological and thematic analysis, participatory methods and literature reviews. She additionally writes on interprofessional education, academic-practice collaboration and parent-focused oral health interventions for young children.

name: Simone Grassini
summary: Simone Grassini studies how people perceive, trust and use artificial intelligence, drawing on psychometric scale development and validation, surveys, and preregistered online experiments. Applications include AI in higher education and military training, AI ethics, social robots, digital health acceptance and comparisons of AI and human creativity. He also works on environmental psychology and visual consciousness, using bibliometric mapping, implicit association tests and mental imagery tasks.

name: Siv Oltedal
summary: Siv Oltedal studies frontline social work and welfare administration in Norway, especially how Nav caseworkers use discretion and room for action when rules, resources and clients' needs pull in different directions. Her work uses qualitative and interactional methods, including analysis of recorded client-worker conversations, a client-feedback system, focus groups with case vignettes and international comparison, alongside legal and theoretical perspectives. Topics include care and control, user involvement, welfare-to-work, non-discrimination, digital guidance and cultural diversity in social work.

name: Sjur Skjørshammer Sætren
summary: Sjur Skjørshammer Sætren studies how childhood maltreatment and other adversities relate to adolescent mental and somatic health, emotion regulation and affective inhibitory control, mainly using the large Norwegian UEVO population survey of 12–16 year olds. His work uses generalized linear models, latent change score and mediation models, network analysis, and questionnaire validation, and also includes a systematic review of adversity measurement in psychosis research, a study of remission in clinical high risk of psychosis, a physiological study of emotion regulation and self-efficacy, and a longitudinal study of adolescent health during the COVID-19 pandemic.

name: Svein Erik Tuastad
summary: Svein Erik Tuastad studies how public welfare and security institutions operate in practice, with a focus on Norwegian child welfare services and social work. His publications use qualitative methods such as focus groups and in-depth interviews to examine how child welfare staff weigh family reunification and children's needs after European Court of Human Rights rulings, and how social workers cooperate with police and the security service in preventing radicalisation and violent extremism. He also writes on politics, public debate, religious schooling, citizen attitudes and research evaluation in Norway.

name: Thiago Medeiros da Costa Daniele
summary: Thiago Medeiros da Costa Daniele studies physical activity, mental health and well-being across the life course, with a focus on university students, older adults and teachers in Brazil. His work uses systematic and integrative reviews, meta-analysis, bibliometric mapping, cross-sectional surveys with regression, psychometric validation and critical policy analysis. Application areas include public health, gerontology, exercise and fitness programming, preclinical research on exercise and sleep deprivation, and social media psychology.

name: Tina Bojovic
summary: Tina Bojovic conducts qualitative social work research on young adults who grow up between minority and majority cultures in Norway. Using in-depth interviews and perspectives such as intersectionality and social constructivism, her work examines othering, belonging, the role of alcohol, and social control in friendships and romantic relationships. Her findings question framings that locate social control only within immigrant families and have been shared in journal articles, a doctoral thesis and talks in Norway and abroad.

name: Vanessa Heaslip
summary: Vanessa Heaslip conducts research on the nursing and midwifery workforce, covering academic careers, advanced practice roles, retention in emergency and social care, and digital health leadership. She also works on health inequalities for marginalised groups, including Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities and decolonising midwifery education, and on patient experience in clinical trials of burn scar, hip and ankle treatments and a heritage-based social prescribing programme for mental health. Her methods include systematic, scoping and integrative reviews, qualitative interviews and focus groups, mixed-methods surveys, concept analysis, and randomised trials with economic evaluation.

name: Wenche Hovland
summary: Wenche Hovland studies social work and child welfare in Norway, with a focus on sibling relationships among children and young people who have experienced parental divorce or been taken into care by child protection services. Using mainly qualitative methods such as semi-structured interviews, thematic analysis and integrative literature review, the work also examines the expectations of unaccompanied refugee minors and social work leaders in trauma-informed residential care. Further publications address academic-practice collaboration through podcasting and give practice recommendations for social workers and other supportive adults.

name: Live Kolstad Kvalsvik
department: Faculty of Social Sciences (department not stated)

name: Ole Madsen
department: Faculty of Social Sciences (department not stated)
summary: Ole Madsen is listed as the author of a 2023 Norwegian-language piece commemorating Mari Høgestøl (1954-2023), a memorial tribute rather than a research article. The single publication provided contains no information on research topics, methods or application areas, so his scholarly expertise cannot be described from this record.

name: Thomas Andre Ims
department: Faculty of Social Sciences (department not stated)
summary: Thomas Andre Ims studies how families and communities with minority and migration backgrounds experience belonging, identity and access to support. His publications look at how parents in interethnic families think about their children's future sense of self when choosing a kindergarten, and report findings from dialogue cafés on grief support for adult refugees. The work draws on participatory, dialogue-based approaches and addresses social services, municipalities, and faith and minority organisations.

name: Antoinette Harmke De Lange
department: NHS – Department of Leadership and Service Innovation
summary: Antoinette Harmke De Lange studies ageing workforces, sustainable employability and sustainable careers, covering topics such as bridge employment, job crafting, wise proactivity, career shocks and age-related stereotypes. Her work uses surveys, longitudinal and observational studies, scale validation, latent class analysis, interviews and systematic reviews. It is applied mainly in healthcare, elderly care and freight transport, with attention to HR policy, workplace health promotion and intervention implementation.

name: Aaron Martin Cooper
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Aaron Martin Cooper studies how international and national law can protect Indigenous rights in the Arctic as the climate changes and new interventions are proposed. His work uses doctrinal and critical environmental law analysis, drawing on case law and treaty body practice, to examine geoengineering such as sea ice thickening and solar radiation management, with a focus on Sámi participatory rights in Norway, Sweden and Finland. He also proposes legal standards, including a consent framework for geoengineering, and considers Arctic Ocean governance and climate justice.

name: Andrea Minto
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Andrea Minto studies EU financial regulation, with a focus on anti-money laundering supervision, crypto-assets and stablecoins, central bank digital currencies, and banking regulation. His work uses doctrinal legal analysis, sometimes supported by institutional and complexity-theory frameworks, to examine the new EU AML authority, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, payment services rules and the legal role of central banks. Application areas include bank internal governance, payment providers, professional football, crypto exchange platforms and securities post-trading technology.

name: Annette AlstadsÃ¦ter
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Annette Alstadsæter studies tax compliance, tax evasion and enforcement, and the distribution of income and wealth, mainly using linked Norwegian administrative register data on individuals and firms. Her work uses reform-based empirical analysis and economic modelling to examine tax penalties, offshore wealth and automatic exchange of bank information, and the measurement of top income shares including business income. She also contributes policy analyses and consultation responses on tax rules, financial crime detection and information sharing between banks and public authorities.

name: Benn Folkvord
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Benn Folkvord works in Norwegian tax law, covering corporate and capital taxation, tax planning, and the limits of tax rules in relation to private law and constitutional and EEA law. His publications use legal doctrinal analysis to examine topics such as whether private law arrangements can be set aside under an unwritten attribution principle, the participation exemption, exit taxation, and the cost of complying with tax rules. He also addresses the retroactivity ban in the Norwegian Constitution, the tax treatment of repaid equity, and the history of tax law, and has contributed a consultation response on paid-in capital rules.

name: Bård Misund
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Bård Misund studies the economics of Norwegian salmon aquaculture, including industry clusters and agglomeration, offshore production strategies, disease costs, profitability under environmental regulation and the effects of rent taxation on company returns. He also analyses resource rent taxation and investment neutrality in Norwegian oil and gas. His methods include difference-in-differences estimation, profit-persistence models, economic and investment analysis and disaggregated production data, and his work extends to policy consultation responses and regional reports on sea lice reduction and fish health economics.

name: Dengjun Zhang
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Dengjun Zhang is an applied economist who studies seafood markets and firm behaviour, focusing on salmon demand, consumer preference shifts, price transmission and the economics of salmon farming. He uses econometric methods such as demand systems, hedonic price models, profit-persistence models, instrumental variables and Google Trends data, and applies them to household and auction data as well as to large cross-country firm surveys. His work also covers manufacturing and sustainability topics, including energy outages, credit constraints, green innovation, environmental activities of firms, temporary employment and climate-related behaviour.

name: Eivind Furuseth
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Eivind Furuseth works on Norwegian tax law, with a focus on how complex tax rules affect the costs of compliance for taxpayers and businesses. His publications include commentary on the burden of following tax rules, the effects of deduction rules on entrepreneurs, and exit taxation. He also compiles tax law collections used as teaching materials for students.

name: Erika Christie Berle
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Erika Christie Berle studies sustainable finance, corporate governance and the energy transition using quantitative methods such as regression analysis, asset pricing tests and text analysis. Her work examines how ethical exclusions by the Norwegian Oil Fund and ESG considerations relate to stock returns, cost of capital and firm behaviour, including Nordic IPOs. She also analyses how gender composition shapes committee and board deliberations, and how regional news narratives relate to wind turbine presence and public attitudes in Germany.

name: Gert Johan Kjelby
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Gert Johan Kjelby works in Norwegian criminal procedure law and police law, combining legal-historical analysis with article-by-article commentary on the Criminal Procedure Act. His publications trace how Norwegian criminal procedure legislation developed from the 1687 Norwegian Law through the 1887 reform to the current 1981 act, and they examine specific police powers such as bringing a person to a police station. He also writes about how police law texts have developed from a practical craft into an academic discipline.

name: Hamid Cheraghali
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Hamid Cheraghali studies financial distress and default prediction for small and medium-sized enterprises, using logistic regression and machine learning methods such as LightGBM and XGBoost on Norwegian and U.S. firm data, and has also reviewed the methodological literature in this area. He also works in empirical finance, using event analysis, volatility forecasting and Google search data to examine how cyberattacks, investor fear and consumer or investor attention relate to returns, volatility and fund flows in cryptocurrency, oil, luxury-goods and mutual fund markets.

name: Helle Austvik Tholo
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Helle Austvik Tholo researches Norwegian tax law, focusing on when losses, especially lost monetary claims, can be deducted. Using doctrinal legal analysis and a Scandinavian comparison of Norway, Sweden and Denmark, she examines the conditions of business activity, profit capacity, own account and risk, and the dividing line between active business and passive capital investment, including the debt-equity boundary and working shareholders. She also takes part in public debate on wealth tax and in legal education.

name: Kristine Gullhav Hansen
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Kristine Gullhav Hansen studies Norwegian procedural law, with a focus on the Supreme Court's authority to review appraisal decisions made in expropriation and similar cases. Her work, based on the provisions of the Norwegian Appraisal Procedure Act (skjønnsprosessloven) section 38, uses legal analysis of the statute and how it is applied to examine how far the highest court can reassess a second-instance appraisal. The topic is relevant to the judiciary, public authorities and landowners involved in compensation and property valuation disputes.

name: Kristoffer Svendsen
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Kristoffer Svendsen works across two distinct fields: energy and petroleum law, and laser-plasma physics. His legal research covers environmental impact assessment in climate litigation, liability and risk allocation in upstream oil and gas, offshore wind contracts and project finance, and LNG export regulation. His experimental and simulation work on laser wakefield accelerators, using Bayesian optimization, plasma lenses and particle-in-cell modelling, aims to improve electron beam quality and produce x-rays for absorption spectroscopy and spray tomography.

name: Lana Bubalo
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Lana Bubalo studies legal questions around data protection, personality rights and online harms, including GDPR non-material damages in the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, the legal history of honor and reputation, and liability for hate speech and discrimination on online platforms. Her work also covers artificial intelligence and law (health sector, data ownership, comparative law), consumer law such as the EU right to repair, and the legal cultures of the Western Balkans. Methods are doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, cross-country surveys and historical review, together with writing on legal education.

name: Marie Larsen Gellein
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Marie Larsen Gellein researches Norwegian insolvency law, with a focus on the principle of equal treatment of creditors in bankruptcy. Her work, published in 2024, appears to be legal-doctrinal, examining how this principle operates within bankruptcy proceedings. The topic is relevant to creditors, insolvency practitioners and courts.

name: Marius Sikveland
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Marius Sikveland studies corporate finance, focusing on how firms fund themselves and how financing choices relate to profitability, using econometric analysis of firm-level panel data. His work covers political connections and access to government support and bank loans during COVID-19, ownership and profitability in Norwegian salmon aquaculture, and capital structure in the hospitality industry under seasonality and geographic clustering. The applications span crisis policy, aquaculture and tourism.

name: Ola Johan Settem
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Ola Johan Settem works in Norwegian and European public and human rights law, including freedom of religion, academic freedom of expression and judicial impartiality. His publications combine doctrinal legal analysis, proportionality analysis of European Court of Human Rights case law and comparison with other international tribunals. He also writes article-by-article statutory commentaries on Norwegian laws covering elections, impeachment procedure, folk high schools and ritual circumcision of boys.

name: Roger Stelander Magnussen
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Roger Stelander Magnussen works in Norwegian property and procedural law, with a main focus on land registration (tinglysing) and the law on the extinction of rights. His publications are mainly article-by-article legal commentaries on the Norwegian Land Registration Act and the Act on redemption rights (løsningsrett), along with studies on procedural extinction and loss of rights through passivity in co-ownership situations. He has also written on Norwegian church law literature and contributed to Festschrift volumes.

name: Son Tha Huynh
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Son Tha Huynh studies finance topics at the intersection of corporate financing and market behavior. One line of work applies natural language processing (BERT) and machine learning methods such as random forests to earnings call transcripts of S&P 500 firms to forecast stock market reactions and risk. Another line examines how political, environmental and crisis-related uncertainty shapes firms' debt financing and leverage decisions.

name: Tarjei Mandt Larsen
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Tarjei Mandt Larsen is a philosopher whose published work centres on epistemology and phenomenology, especially Husserl's accounts of perceptual justification, perceptual givenness and the problem of how knowledge of mind-independent objects is possible. His method is close conceptual and textual analysis of Husserl's arguments, set against current debates in the epistemology of perception and metaepistemology. He also works on research integrity and trust in research, as a research ombud who takes part in discussions on academic freedom and the conditions for research.

name: Vegard Bø Bahus
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Vegard Bø Bahus works in Norwegian and Nordic law, with a focus on animal law, civil procedure and strategic litigation. His publications include a case study of a Norwegian Supreme Court judgment on dog breeding and a contribution to a volume on animal welfare and rights in the Nordic countries. He has also written on the legal framework for compulsory mental health care for patients who have decision-making capacity but pose a danger to their own lives, and on rules for residence linked to work and study.

name: William Gilje Gjedrem
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: William Gilje Gjedrem works on oral health among marginalized populations, with a focus on people living in prisons. The publication describes a multicenter randomized, double-blinded controlled trial in four prisons in Rogaland County testing whether motivational interviewing added to oral hygiene packages improves plaque scores, hygiene routines and related attitudes. The work is relevant to correctional services, dental practitioners and policy makers planning dental care for underserved groups.

name: Alessandra Piazza
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Alessandra Piazza designs large-scale, multi-country survey experiments in Europe to study how citizens perceive and accept nature-based solutions to climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. Her approach combines randomized vignette experiments, information-provision treatments and stated-preference methods, including referendum-style questions and household willingness-to-pay elicitation. The work is aimed at informing environmental policy design by comparing public support across countries and across types of benefits, costs and required behaviour.

name: Anders Åkerman
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Anders Åkerman studies international trade, firm behaviour and labour markets, mainly using Swedish and Norwegian employer-employee and firm-level data with causal estimation strategies and theoretical models of heterogeneous firms. His work covers how importing affects firms' carbon intensity, how market concentration and technology shape demand for college-educated workers, how broadband changes the effect of distance on trade, and how workers spread knowledge between firms. He has also analysed the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on Swedish firms and workers, including firm support measures, and has written commentary on tariffs and exchange rates.

name: Antik Debnath
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Antik Debnath studies sustainability from both an energy-engineering and an economics perspective. His work includes techno-economic modelling of rooftop solar and electric vehicle charging in a university campus microgrid, and survey and econometric studies (PLS-SEM, fsQCA, wavelet coherence, panel and time-series models) on digital financial inclusion, financial development, climate action, CO2 emissions and environmental behaviour. Application areas include Bangladesh, MENA countries and campus energy systems, with a focus on policy implications for sustainable development.

name: Bernt Arne Ødegaard
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Bernt Arne Ødegaard studies empirical finance, covering stock market liquidity and trading, ethical and ESG-based investing, insider trading and corporate boards, and household borrowing decisions. His work uses large datasets, including Norwegian student loan records, insider trades, trading venue data and fund exclusion lists, together with return-based asset pricing tests and event-based analysis of regulatory changes. Application areas include market structure and tick size rules, margin requirements during COVID-19, board gender quotas, sovereign wealth fund divestment and the reliability of research results across analyst teams.

name: Dora Zsuzsanna Simon
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Dora Zsuzsanna Simon studies the intersection of international trade and environmental policy, using quantitative trade models to examine how climate policies affect countries differently. Her work covers carbon pricing and its distributional effects across countries, environmental comparative advantage, trade-related emissions, and the environmental consequences of meat production and consumption. The research informs questions of fairness, international transfers and sustainable globalization in global climate action.

name: Elin Svensen
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Elin Svensen studies how students' beliefs about whether intelligence is fixed or can grow, known as mindset, relate to school achievement, completion of upper secondary school and educational inequality in Norway. Her quantitative work applies multilevel modeling to survey data on about 10,000 students linked with school and national registry records. She examines differences by family background, gender and classroom environment, and how these relate to students' academic choices and outcomes.

name: Eric Perry Bettinger
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Eric Perry Bettinger studies education and the economics of education, mainly through randomized field experiments and quasi-experimental policy evaluations, along with some survey and machine learning work. His projects cover socioemotional skills and growth mindset, informational and text-message nudges, computer-assisted learning, school day length, and college access, financial aid, dual enrollment and degree completion in the U.S., Brazil and Norway. He also works on research methods, including monitoring of trial fidelity, SMS-based measurement of student mindsets, and satellite imagery as a proxy for regional economic activity.

name: Fuchen Zhang
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Fuchen Zhang works in applied econometrics and production economics, focusing on how firms substitute between inputs and how technological change that favours particular inputs can be identified and measured. Using production-function estimation methods, including a bridging estimator, and firm-level data from Norwegian manufacturing, the work examines substitution between clean and dirty energy and the productivity effects of Covid-19 transfers to firms. Further publications address how agricultural technical change relates to deforestation and how substitution structures can be identified from data.

name: Gerhard Töws
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Gerhard Töws studies labour market consequences of the energy transition, focusing on what happens to workers who lose jobs when coal mining declines. Using the collapse of the UK coal industry as a case study, the research estimates long-run changes in wages, earnings and employment among displaced miners. The work informs policy on the costs borne by workers in coal-dependent regions.

name: Gorm Kipperberg
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Gorm Kipperberg studies how people value the environment and respond to environmental policy, mainly through stated-preference surveys such as discrete choice experiments and contingent valuation, analysed with mixed logit and related models. His work covers marine and coastal ecosystems, mining, wind energy, nature-based solutions, pharmaceutical pollution and aviation emissions, and also examines how survey design, choice architecture and the passage of time affect results. Other publications include meta-analysis, local acceptance and legitimacy of green-transition projects, and spatial and econometric analyses of biogas potential and agricultural carbon emissions.

name: Hammad Shaikh
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Hammad Shaikh studies how email messages and reminders affect student behaviour in computing courses, using randomized A/B experiments, field deployments, surveys and interviews. This work examines homework completion, procrastination, email open rates and exam performance in introductory CS1 classes. He is also listed on a 2025 field experiment on leadership training in grocery stores, which looks at supportive leadership behaviours, work satisfaction, engagement and productivity.

name: Ingeborg Foldøy Solli
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Ingeborg Foldøy Solli studies how early childhood and school-based programs shape children's and adolescents' skills, using randomized field experiments in Norway. Her work covers structured and play-based preschool curricula, executive functions and school readiness, gender gaps in early learning, and school programs teaching coping and growth-mindset skills. Outcomes examined include mathematics, language, mental health, course choices and academic achievement, with some work combining experimental data with skill-formation models.

name: Jean Paul Rabanal Sobrino
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Jean Paul Rabanal Sobrino studies financial markets and decision-making, mainly through laboratory experiments on how exchange-traded funds, index inclusion, stock splits and shareholder voting affect asset prices, trading and corporate policies. He also examines individual choice using experiments on portfolio choice, market entry and exit under different information, and equilibrium play in games, and has used national register data on Norwegian student loans to study how financial knowledge shapes fixed versus variable interest rate choices.

name: Jonas Hveding Hamang
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Jonas Hveding Hamang works on the economics of climate policy, with a focus on policies that act on the supply side of fossil fuels, such as taxing oil production, and on how these affect global CO2 emissions. His publications also address the link between fossil fuel resources and political regimes, including the role of oil in sustaining dictatorships. The work is presented in economics conferences and seminars and in Norwegian-language public outlets, and appears to rely on quantitative economic analysis.

name: Kristoffer Wigestrand Eriksen
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Kristoffer Wigestrand Eriksen studies how people behave when giving financial advice while their own interests conflict with those of the person advised. He uses large-scale behavioral experiments, including a binary dictator game adapted to an advice-giving setting, to compare advisor behavior with a baseline of direct decision-making. His work addresses moral behavior and fairness in financial advice markets.

name: Lassi Mikael Ahlvik
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Lassi Mikael Ahlvik is an environmental and public economist whose work covers climate and resource policy, taxation and innovation. He combines theoretical models, calibration and quasi-experimental or field-experimental methods using firm-level, property-transaction and smartphone-tracking data. Application areas include carbon pricing and green innovation, oil sector taxation and investment, nature conservation and land values, transport behavior, and the climate effects of wood-based products.

name: Lijun Liu
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Lijun Liu studies the economics and sustainability of aquaculture and related natural-resource sectors, using stochastic bioeconomic simulation, sustainability indicator frameworks, cross-case comparisons and regression analysis of survey data. Work covers financial risk in land-based shrimp farming, environmental, economic and social performance of aquaculture systems in China and worldwide, and gender participation in seafood systems. Other publications address public acceptance of wind power in Norwegian municipalities, Chinese consumer attitudes to certified wood, and the trade and processing effects of fishery moratoria.

name: Magne Mogstad
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Magne Mogstad works in labor and public economics, studying how income taxation shapes work decisions and how disability insurance enrollment has changed over time. His publications also cover income equality in the Nordic countries, where he assesses common claims about the Nordic model and draws policy lessons, and they include a paper on green waste and a commentary on Norwegian AI policy. His work relies on empirical analysis of economic and policy data to inform tax, social insurance and welfare policy.

name: Marco Lambrecht
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Marco Lambrecht conducts experimental economics research on financial markets, strategic interaction and decision-making under risk. His laboratory and online experiments examine how Bitcoin-style mining affects price bubbles, how disclosing players' intelligence changes cooperation and coordination in repeated games, and how gender relates to participation in risky skill games. The work informs understanding of cryptocurrency pricing, behavioral game theory and gender differences in risk-taking.

name: Mari Rege
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Mari Rege studies how social and emotional skills and early learning environments shape educational and work outcomes, with a focus on Norway. She mainly runs large-scale field experiments and randomized trials, and also uses register and survey data and skill-formation models, to evaluate curricula, classroom staffing, teacher relationship skills, mental health and coping programs in preschools and schools. Her work extends to leadership training in workplaces and to socioeconomic gaps in children's skills.

name: Olga A. Rud
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Olga A. Rud conducts laboratory experiments in finance and economics, studying how asset prices, trading volume and market behavior respond to market structure and information. Her work covers exchange-traded fund indexing and index inclusion, stock splits, shareholder trading and voting on firm policies with externalities, and dynamic portfolio choice, and she also tests game-theoretic ideas such as correlated equilibrium and entry decisions under public versus private information. Methods combine controlled experiments, formal modeling and nonparametric efficiency tests, with relevance to asset pricing, corporate governance and sustainable investing.

name: Peter Molnar
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Peter Molnar studies financial econometrics and empirical finance, with a focus on volatility modelling and forecasting using range-based GARCH and multivariate correlation models, including applications to cryptocurrencies, oil and exchange rates. He also develops and compares statistical and machine learning methods (logit, LightGBM, XGBoost) for predicting SME default and financial distress, and uses difference-in-differences and event-style analyses to examine how taxes, infrastructure, cyberattacks and investor or consumer attention affect asset and house prices.

name: Radoslaw Lucjan Stefanski
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Radoslaw Lucjan Stefanski works in economics, covering the social discount rate used to appraise public investments and the taxation and resource allocation of the oil industry. One paper uses a Ramsey-style framework, with attention to long-run interest rates and differences in patience across generations, and applies it to the UK Green Book's approach to cost-benefit analysis. The other publication, listed with no abstract, studies misallocation and tax wedges in oil extraction.

name: Sadaf Basharat
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Sadaf Basharat studies measurement and educational equity, using quantitative methods on survey and large-scale assessment data. One line of work tests and refines the psychometric properties of a workplace well-being questionnaire for early childhood education and care staff in Norway, using factor analysis and reliability and validity checks on trial data. Another analyses TIMSS 2019 data with regression models and Fisher's exact test to compare school climate and student intake across boys', girls' and mixed schools in single-sex education systems.

name: Shuqi Wang
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Shuqi Wang studies behavioral and household finance, focusing on how investors and borrowers make decisions under differing information costs and levels of financial sophistication. The publications use large transaction and repayment datasets, along with natural-experiment designs such as the rollout of the EDGAR filing system, to examine retail investor overconfidence, trading performance of foreign versus domestic investors, and fixed versus variable interest-rate choices in student loans. Application areas include stock markets, investor behavior, and consumer debt.

name: Simone  Haeckl
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Simone Haeckl is a behavioral and experimental economist who studies gender gaps, motivation and decision-making using randomized field experiments, online and lab experiments, and surveys. Her work covers children's interest in STEM and the methodology of school experiments, leadership training and team incentives in workplaces, competition and self-assessment, and investor responses to sustainability information. Applications span education, labour markets, organisational management and sustainable finance.

name: Sophie Agnes Marie Cottet
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Sophie Agnes Marie Cottet studies how firms respond to labor-cost policies and public transfers, focusing on payroll tax reductions for minimum-wage workers in France and Covid-19 support to firms in Norway. Her work uses administrative employer-employee data to examine employment growth, rent sharing, liquidity and credit constraints, the salience of labor-cost reductions, and productivity effects. She has also contributed to policy discussions and an official hearing on payroll tax reductions and the State's role in funding and regulating firms.

name: Sufyan Ullah Khan
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Sufyan Ullah Khan studies the economics of carbon reduction, environmental efficiency and sustainable development, mainly in China and also in Pakistan. The work uses panel econometrics (threshold, spatial and time-series models), decomposition and stochastic frontier analysis, interpretable machine learning, and stated-preference surveys. Application areas include urban form and emissions, marine fisheries, agriculture, mining, green finance, air pollution and well-being, biogas siting, and willingness to pay for environmental services.

name: Torfinn Harding
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Torfinn Harding studies environmental and public economics, with a focus on deforestation, resource extraction and taxation. His work uses spatial and satellite data, firm-level datasets and quasi-experimental methods such as difference-in-differences to assess conditional cash transfers in the Brazilian Amazon, the effect of governance on forest loss from oil drilling, and how the timing of tax deductions affects petroleum investment in Norway and the UK. He also writes on corporate taxation, Covid support to firms and climate policy, and has contributed editorial and public commentary pieces.

name: Venke Furre Haaland
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Venke Furre Haaland studies the economics of education and health, using field experiments, randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental variation. Her work examines how extra classroom teachers, teacher professional development and digital parent-focused interventions affect children's learning, and how waiting times for orthopedic surgery affect patients' work absence and disability receipt. She has also contributed to local work on social exclusion and an app for young people outside upper secondary education.

name: Wanwei He
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Wanwei He studies how ethically motivated investment exclusions affect stock returns and corporate behavior, using the divestment decisions of Norway's sovereign wealth fund as an empirical setting. The work uses asset pricing methods to estimate return premiums for excluded and re-included firms and to test whether the fund's actions directly drive these patterns. It also examines how excluded companies change their operations in response, with relevance to ESG investing and cost of capital.

name: Yuko Onozaka
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
summary: Yuko Onozaka studies how gender and diversity shape organizational outcomes, and how consumers make food choices. Her work uses regression analysis, linguistic analysis of meeting transcripts, choice experiments with latent class analysis, and think-aloud protocols combined with text mining. Application areas include central bank committee deliberations, women in leadership and digital transformation, and consumer preferences for farmed salmon in the USA, France and Japan.

name: Alberto Giacometti
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Alberto Giacometti studies regional development and policy governance, focusing on how transformative innovation policy, just green transition planning and green industrial strategies are designed and carried out in Nordic and Western Balkan regions. His work uses policy review, interviews, focus groups and conceptual analysis through lenses such as territorial governance and experimentalist governance. He also takes part in stakeholder workshops with firms, public bodies and researchers on battery and green industry development in Norwegian regions.

name: Aldijana Bunjak
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Aldijana Bunjak studies organizational behavior, focusing on identity leadership, employee well-being and innovation at work. Her work uses large multi-country and multi-source surveys, longitudinal and multilevel designs, structural equation modeling, latent profile analysis and bibliometric review. It examines how leadership, trust, mindfulness, digital technology and job design relate to outcomes such as burnout, exhaustion, citizenship behavior, creativity, job performance and academics' career intentions.

name: Ali Turkyilmaz
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Ali Turkyilmaz studies circular economy adoption in the construction industry, looking at costs and benefits, barriers, policy, digital tools and circularity assessment frameworks, mainly through stakeholder surveys, interviews, case studies and literature reviews. He also researches Industry 4.0 readiness and digital transformation in manufacturing and enterprises in emerging economies such as Kazakhstan, and supply chain topics including additive manufacturing, digital inventory and simulation of spare-part repair for oil and gas operations. Further work uses structural equation modelling and data envelopment analysis to examine remote work and education in residential environments and the innovation performance of universities.

name: Andra Riandita
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Andra Riandita studies how firms pursue sustainability and eco-innovation through partnerships, collaboration and reporting, with a focus on food, textile/fashion and energy supply chains. The work uses quantitative analysis of firm survey data, qualitative comparative analysis, content analysis of partnership portfolios, interviews and case studies. Applied projects examine digital tools and verification for SME sustainability data collection under emerging EU reporting rules, and other studies compare how firm location affects collaboration for eco-innovation.

name: Andrada Iazmina Farcau
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Andrada Iazmina Farcau studies how growth and restructuring in the defence sector affect regional development, with a focus on peripheral regions. Her publications, all titled around a "camouflage green transition", examine whether expanding defence activity benefits the regions that host it and how existing regional trajectories shape the outcomes. The work belongs to regional economic development and economic geography, and it is relevant to regional policy and industrial strategy.

name: Andres Rodriguez Pose
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Andres Rodriguez Pose studies how institutions, innovation and place shape regional development and territorial inequality, with a focus on the EU, China and other regions. His publications use panel econometrics, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, latent class and decision-tree models, as well as literature reviews and policy analysis. Application areas include EU Cohesion Policy, industrial policy, urban agglomeration, digital and AI technologies, the geography of science, and the political geography of discontent.

name: Annie Haver
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Annie Haver studies resilience, stress and mental wellbeing among older adult care workers, informal caregivers, and students in nursing and higher education. Her work uses systematic and qualitative reviews, interviews, cross-sectional surveys with moderation analyses, and a mixed-methods co-design project across seven countries to develop a digital toolbox for care leaders. She also examines emotion regulation and emotional intelligence in relation to stress and mental distress, and leadership competencies in the Norwegian hotel industry.

name: Auke Hunneman
faculty: UiS School of Business and Law
department: Department of Innovation, Management and Marketing
summary: Auke Hunneman studies consumer and firm behavior in marketing and retail using quantitative models, including hierarchical Bayesian regression, spatial panel data models and survey experiments.
